A merchant travelling north left someone with authority over his goods, his debts and his household, and that man answered for what happened in his absence. The role carried power and exposure together. To say he is not that for them told the audience precisely which relationship was not on offer.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a settled resting place in this ayah appears elsewhere in the Quran for the earth as a dwelling and for the sun's course, so it belongs to the vocabulary of things reaching their appointed position. Applied to news, it treats a report as something travelling toward a location rather than merely being true or false.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is divided cleanly: the message is delivered, the response belongs to those receiving it, and the timing belongs to God. That division is what makes long, unrewarded work sustainable, and the Quran gives it to a messenger before giving it to anyone else. The second ayah adds the piece that makes trust possible, which is that resolution is located rather than merely promised. It has somewhere to arrive.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same line: whoever is guided is guided for himself, and he is not a keeper over them.
States the limit of the office in two clauses: you are a reminder, and not one who controls them.
Repeats the release if they turn away, since he was not sent as a guardian over them.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been carrying that belongs to someone else: a decision, a habit, a life you cannot live for them. Say the sentence out loud, that you are not the keeper of this. Then name the one part that is genuinely yours and do that. Setting a thing down properly requires knowing what remains in your hands.

studies.title: Until They Change The Subject
studies.meaning: The instruction is unusually practical. When people are wading into talk about God's signs, withdraw, and the condition for returning is stated exactly: until they move to another topic. Commentators note that no argument is prescribed and no confrontation. Then a provision is made for forgetting, which assumes it will happen. The second ayah relieves the withdrawing person of any account for the others, and gives the whole instruction a purpose that is about them rather than against them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the setting is social rather than formal. Mockery of the recitation happened in gatherings where believers were present, sometimes as entertainment. The classical commentators describe believers being drawn into defending the Quran in rooms where nothing was being decided. This ayah addresses that situation, and a Medinan passage later repeats the instruction in almost identical terms.

keyTerms.note: The verb for walking into water without knowing its depth. Used of talk, it names the kind of confident discussion that goes further than anybody's knowledge, which is why the Quran picks it for careless speech about God.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for those who turned from the signs. Here it is given as an instruction, so a word describing a fault becomes, in a different setting, a discipline.
Used twice in this passage with two senses: the recollection that ends forgetfulness, and the reminder offered to others. One word covers remembering yourself and being remembered to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan evenings were spent in company. Men gathered by the sanctuary or in a courtyard and talk moved through poetry, news and jokes, with reputations made and lost by what someone said well. Leaving such a gathering was noticed. The instruction here has a social cost built into it, which is why the ayah names the exact condition under which you can sit back down.
studies.didYouKnow: This instruction appears twice in the Quran, once here in a Meccan surah and once later in a Medinan one, using the same verb for wading into talk and the same condition about waiting for another subject. The Medinan version adds a clause about becoming like them, which the earlier version leaves unstated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats company as formative rather than neutral. Where you sit shapes what you become used to hearing, and the remedy offered is physical distance rather than a better argument. It also assumes human weakness gracefully: forgetting is anticipated and answered with an instruction for afterwards, not a reprimand. And it keeps the purpose oriented toward the others, since the reminder is offered in hope, not in judgement.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction in a Medinan setting, with the same condition about waiting for another topic.
Describes those who pass by empty talk with dignity, as a settled quality rather than a single choice.
Shows the same withdrawal from idle speech, with a courteous parting rather than a quarrel.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next conversation, online or in a room, where people are being clever about something sacred and nobody knows much. You do not need to correct anyone. Leave, or close the tab, and come back when the subject has changed. The ayah gives a condition for returning, which makes this a pause rather than a rupture.

studies.title: Religion As A Pastime
studies.meaning: Two words describe what has been done with religion: it has become play and diversion. Commentators read this as covering both those who mocked and those who kept the forms without weight. The instruction is to leave them, followed at once by an instruction to keep reminding, so withdrawal is not abandonment. The reason given is the danger of a soul being handed over to what it earned, with no ally, no intercessor, and no ransom accepted however much is offered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage about who can be reached and how. The city's religious life was genuinely festive: seasonal fairs, poetry contests, rites around the sanctuary that doubled as entertainment and commerce. Describing that as play and diversion was not an exaggeration invented for the argument. It named the arrangement the city itself would have recognised.

keyTerms.note: Activity done for its own amusement, the word used of children's games. Applied to religion it says the practice is real and the seriousness is missing, which is a sharper charge than hypocrisy.
From a root for being taken in by an appearance, used of a market deal that looked better than it was. The deceiver is named as the present life itself rather than any person.

keyTerms.gloss: it is given up, handed over
keyTerms.note: A rare verb, appearing only in this ayah in the Quran, twice. Commentators gloss it as being consigned or held in pledge, and the range of their explanations reflects how uncommon the word is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was an ordinary transaction. A captive taken in a raid was valued and bought back, and a killing could be settled with an agreed number of camels rather than blood. Every family understood the arithmetic and most had used it. The statement that no equivalent will be accepted removes the one mechanism the audience relied on for undoing what could not be undone.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing a soul being handed over occurs nowhere else in the Quran except in this single ayah, where it appears twice. Rare words of this kind are the ones the earliest philological works on the Quran spent most effort explaining, and the commentaries preserve several proposed meanings side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Seriousness is treated as part of what religion is, so that keeping the shape while dropping the weight is described as a change in kind rather than a matter of degree. The passage also completes the surah's argument about intermediaries by closing the last door, which is payment. Nothing can be substituted for a person at that point, which makes what a life actually contained the only thing available.

crossReferences.why: Names the present life as play, amusement and adornment, then shows what remains of it.
Uses the same verb of deception, warning against being taken in by the present life and by the deceiver.
States the same refusal of ransom: an earth-full of gold would not be accepted from one of them.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what part of your religious life has become comfortable enough to be a routine you enjoy rather than something you mean. Not to give it up. Pick one such practice this week and do it slowly enough to notice what it is for. The ayah is about weight going missing while the shape remains.

studies.title: Turned Back On Our Heels
studies.meaning: The refusal is put as a question about direction. Calling on something that neither helps nor harms would mean turning back on your heels after being guided, which is movement in reverse rather than a change of opinion. Then a picture is drawn: a man led off by devils, wandering bewildered in open country, while companions on the road call him to come to them. Commentators note that the ayah does not say whether he answers. It leaves him mid-scene and turns to the declaration that God's guidance is the guidance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the pressure behind it was real. People who accepted the message were being urged back by families who framed the return as reasonable and as loyalty to their own. The wording answers that framing rather than the theology. No specific occasion is attested, and the surah addresses the situation in several places using different images each time.

keyTerms.note: The plural of heel, used in the idiom for turning back the way you came. It describes reversal as bodily movement, which is why the Quran uses it for abandoning a position rather than for changing a view.
A verb built on the root for falling and for desire. It carries both at once, so the luring described is a downward pull toward what the person already wanted rather than an external abduction.
An intensive form for someone turning in place, unable to choose a direction. It appears only here in the Quran, and it names confusion as a physical state rather than an intellectual one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Getting lost was the standard nightmare of desert travel, and the stories about it were specific: a man who left the fire to check on an animal, circling within a mile of the camp all night while people called his name. Sound carries strangely over dunes. The scene in this ayah, with companions calling from the road and a man turning in place, was a story everyone had heard told.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the bewildered man occurs only once in the entire Quran, in this ayah. Such single occurrences are rare enough that classical scholars catalogued them, and they tend to appear at the vivid centre of a comparison, where an ordinary word would have blurred the picture being drawn.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as a position already occupied rather than a conclusion still being weighed, which changes what leaving it means. The comparison also makes an observation about how people are lost: not seized, but drawn by something they wanted, while help is audible the whole time. And the declaration that follows relocates the standard. Guidance is defined by its source, so the question stops being which road feels right.

crossReferences.why: States the same measure in almost identical words, that God's guidance is the guidance itself.
Describes people who took devils as allies instead of God and reckon that they are guided.
Pictures the reversal differently, as worship on an edge that turns on its face when trouble comes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good practice you have quietly let go of in the last year, and notice how the letting go was argued for at the time. It usually sounds reasonable. Pick that one thing and restart it this week at half its old size. The ayah describes reversal as movement, which means it can be walked back the same way.

studies.title: And To Establish The Prayer
studies.meaning: The ayah completes a sentence begun before it, so the instruction to submit to the Lord of the worlds runs directly into two more: establish the prayer, and be mindful of Him. Commentators note that the verb used with prayer is not simply to perform but to set upright, which suggests keeping something standing rather than executing it. The closing clause supplies the horizon. It is to Him that you will be gathered, and everything before it is oriented by that.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the prayer being described belongs to the earliest period of the community's practice, before its later Medinan detail. The classical sources place regular prayer at the centre of the Meccan believers' life from very early, and much of the harassment they faced came when they were seen praying. The instruction here is joined grammatically to the declarations before it.

keyTerms.note: The causative of standing, used of putting up a structure and of maintaining an institution. It asks for something kept upright over time, which is why the Quran rarely says simply to perform the prayer.
From a root meaning to guard or shield oneself. It describes careful attention to a relationship rather than fear of a person, so the English words for piety and fear both fall short of it.
The same passive used earlier in this surah for being assembled before God. Its reappearance here attaches the two instructions to a destination rather than leaving them as good practice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in prayer was conspicuous in Mecca. There was no separate building and no privacy for it; people prayed in courtyards, at the edge of the sanctuary, in the open where anyone passing could see. Some of the early community went out to the ravines around the city to pray unobserved. The instruction to keep it standing was, in that setting, a public commitment.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran almost always pairs the prayer with the verb for setting something upright rather than with a verb for doing or completing. The construction is consistent enough across Meccan and Medinan passages that the classical grammarians treated the pairing as fixed, and the choice keeps continuity, rather than performance, at the centre of the phrase.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is placed here as the practical shape of the submission just described, so the declaration and the daily action belong to one sentence. That connection matters more than either half alone. The mention of gathering at the end also sets the frame: the practice is not offered as a technique for a better life now but as the ordinary posture of someone who expects to stand somewhere and answer.

crossReferences.why: Gives the prayer a stated purpose in the same imperative form, as a remembrance of God.
Describes what the practice does over time, restraining a person from what is shameful and wrong.
Sets the prayer at the two ends of the day, with good deeds removing what is bad.

studies.applyIt: Choose the prayer in your day that is most rushed, usually the one squeezed against something else, and give it five extra minutes tomorrow. Not more words. Just room around it, so the standing is not immediately followed by moving. The verb in this ayah is about keeping something upright, and things stay upright when they are not knocked into.

studies.title: His Word Is The Truth
studies.meaning: Creation is said to be in truth, meaning with a purpose rather than as a game, and that phrase governs everything after it. Then the mode of creation: a word said, and the thing is. Early scholars note the tense, since the sentence describes a day still ahead while using a present verb, which keeps one act of command over both the first creation and the raising. Sovereignty is then named specifically for the day the trumpet sounds.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It closes a passage that has followed Abraham's argument with his people and then run through a list of prophets. The surah speaks to an audience who accepted God as creator while treating other powers as go-betweens. This verse answers them by leaving no room for a second authority on the day it would matter most. Early scholars report no particular occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: The word covers truth, right and what is due. Saying the heavens were made with it denies that creation is arbitrary, and the same word returns two clauses later to describe God's own speech.
The bare imperative of the verb to be, two letters in Arabic. It is the shortest command the language can form, and the shortness is the point: nothing stands between the intention and the thing.
A curved horn of the kind used to summon people or signal an army. The Quran uses it for the blast that ends and then restarts everything, and here it fixes the moment sovereignty becomes undeniable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Authority in Mecca was spread among the clans by office and by custom. Nobody held all of it. Decisions were taken in assembly. Alliances shifted. The man who looked dominant one season could be outplayed the next. A claim that rule on one particular day belongs to a single holder, with no assembly and no bargaining, described something nobody there had ever seen.
studies.didYouKnow: The command translated as be is a single word of two letters in Arabic. It occurs several times in the Quran, always in the same construction. Each time the answer is given in the same breath. There is no gap between command and result. The grammar itself refuses any interval in which the thing might not yet exist.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation and resurrection are folded into one kind of act. If the first needed nothing but a word, the second cannot be harder. That is the argument the verse makes without stating it. Naming God as knower of both the hidden and the witnessed then closes a gap a listener might use. No area, private or public, is held back from the same authority. The closing names concern wisdom and detail rather than force.

crossReferences.why: States the same command and its instant answer, arguing directly for the resurrection.
Applies the same phrasing to the origination of the heavens and the earth.
Describes the two blasts of the trumpet and what happens between them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you keep postponing because the first step feels heavy. Do the smallest possible version of it within the next hour, not the whole thing. This verse puts no distance between a word and its effect, and while nothing human works that way, most of the distance we experience turns out to be added by us.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth for a reason. When he says to a thing, be, it is. On the day the trumpet sounds, everything will belong to him alone.

studies.title: Do You Take Idols As Gods
studies.meaning: The story opens with a question put to his own father, and the question is not aggressive but incredulous. He then states what he sees, using the word for plain error and including the whole community in it. The second ayah steps back to explain the sequence about to unfold. God was showing him the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those who are certain. What follows is therefore presented as instruction rather than as doubt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and placed immediately after a passage about being called back by one's own people. Abraham's situation matched the early Meccan community's precisely: a person who breaks with the religion of his household. The commentators discuss the name given here for his father, some treating it as his name and others as a title or a second name, and they preserve the difference without resolving it.

keyTerms.note: Specifically shaped figures, distinguished in Arabic usage from unshaped stones set up for worship. The word emphasises manufacture, which is the point of the question being asked.
An intensified form of the word for kingdom, appearing only a few times in the Quran. It names not the things owned but the fact of their being held, which is what he is being shown.
From a root for knowledge that has settled and stopped moving. It names a state rather than an act, and the ayah presents it as the intended outcome of what he is about to be shown.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Breaking with a father's religion in that world meant losing a household, a name and a trade at once. Religion was not a private position but the property of a lineage, kept in the same family that kept the wells and the grazing rights. The Meccan converts hearing this story had made or were making the same break, and the ayah names the person it costs most to confront.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for dominion used in this passage occurs only a handful of times in the Quran, and never for ordinary kingship. It has an intensifying ending that Arabic uses sparingly. Its rarity marks the passage that follows as a distinct kind of seeing, not simply looking at the sky more carefully than usual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty is described as something shown rather than argued into place, which frames the coming sequence with the star, moon and sun as an education rather than a wavering. The passage also establishes that the search begins in opposition to what one was raised in, and that this opposition is spoken respectfully. The question to his father is a question, and it is asked before any conclusion is announced to anybody.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same conversation at length, with its gentleness and its repeated address to his father.
Shows him pressing the question further, asking about images to which his people are devoted.
Preserves his declaration of disowning what they worship, apart from the One who originated him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you believe mainly because it was in the house you grew up in, and it can be small: a view about money, a way of handling conflict. Ask where it came from, once, without deciding anything about it. This passage begins with a question rather than a rejection, and the question is the part worth copying.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: I Do Not Love What Sets
studies.meaning: The reasoning is conducted aloud and the conclusion is reached with a verb of love rather than of logic. He sees a star in the falling dark, says this is my Lord, and when it goes down he says he does not love things that set. Commentators differ over whether he is reasoning his way forward or arguing with his people in their own terms, and both readings are old. Either way, the criterion he applies is attachment, and setting is what disqualifies.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a narrative placed where the surah is arguing about what deserves worship. Star and planet worship was practised in the wider region and known in Arabia, so the sequence begins with a live option rather than a hypothetical one. The classical commentators treat this as the opening move of a demonstration, not a report of Abraham having genuinely believed it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for concealing, from the root that gives the words for a garden, a hidden being and the heart's inner chamber. Night arrives here as a covering laid over him rather than as light departing.
A bright heavenly body, used in Arabic for the wandering ones as well as the fixed. The indefinite form keeps it unnamed, so the argument does not depend on which body it was.
A participle for a body that sinks below the horizon, and by extension for anything that declines and disappears. It is the pivot of the whole sequence, repeated at each stage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Navigation in Arabia was done by stars, and their risings and settings were tracked closely enough to fix the seasons and the timing of journeys. Herdsmen and guides could name individual stars and knew which appeared when. To this audience, a body that sets was not a poetic idea. It was a working fact used every night, and its regularity was exactly what made it useful.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for nightfall here shares its root with the Arabic words for a garden, for the unseen beings mentioned elsewhere in the Quran, and for the shielded inner part of a person. All of them are things covered or hidden from view, which is how the language relates concealment and interiority through one set of letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage introduces love as a test for what may be worshipped, which is unusual in a surah built on argument. What sets cannot be loved rightly, because attachment to something that goes under has its ending built into it. That criterion also reaches past idols. Anything that reliably departs, including status and strength, fails the same test, which is why the sequence is remembered outside its original setting.

crossReferences.why: Continues the sequence with the moon, adding a plea for guidance when it too disappears.
Draws the same conclusion directly: do not bow to the sun or moon, but to the One who made them.
Turns the criterion around, describing love that runs from God toward the one who follows the way.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are currently attached to that you know will not last: a role, a physical capacity, a season of life you are inside. Do not detach from it. Just say clearly to yourself that it sets. The passage does not ask for coldness. It asks you to know which things are on their way down before they go.

studies.title: Unless My Lord Guides Me
studies.meaning: The second stage repeats the first and then changes the ending. The moon rises, is named, and sets, and instead of a statement about love he now says something about himself: without guidance he would be among those who go astray. Commentators note the escalation. He has moved from evaluating an object to recognising his own exposure, and the sentence is conditional rather than confident. The reasoning has produced a prayer before it has produced a conclusion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the middle panel of a three-part sequence that the surah presents as instruction given to Abraham. The moon carried religious weight across the ancient Near East, more than any single star, so this stage raises the stakes from the previous one. The commentators treat the whole sequence as a demonstration for his people rather than a record of belief he actually held.

keyTerms.note: A participle for something breaking into view, used of the moon and sun coming up. The root carries a sense of splitting through, so the rising is pictured as an emergence rather than a smooth arrival.
A conditional particle carrying an oath, so the sentence it opens is sworn rather than supposed. It makes the admission that follows a solemn statement instead of a passing thought.
The same root used through this surah for losing a road, and for what the invented partners do at the end. Applying it to himself puts him in the category he has been describing in others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The lunar month organised everything. Arabs dated debts, fairs, journeys and the sacred months by the moon's phases, and a new crescent sighted from a rooftop began a month for a whole region. It was the most consequential object in the sky for practical life. Watching it set was therefore not a small observation; it was watching the timekeeper of the year go under.
studies.didYouKnow: The three stages of this sequence move from a star to the moon to the sun, in order of increasing brightness, and each stage ends differently: a statement about love, a plea for guidance, and finally a declaration. The escalation is structural, and the middle stage is the only one that is a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty is shown to include a dependent moment. Even the figure the Quran presents as the model of finding God says he would go astray without being guided, and he says it after reasoning correctly rather than before. That places asking at the centre of the search rather than at its beginning. It also makes fear and hope work together: the fear names a real possibility, and the address turns it into a request.

crossReferences.why: Turns the same request into the daily prayer of everyone who recites it, in almost the same terms.
Gives the previous stage, where the criterion applied to the setting star was love rather than a plea.
Records a similar phrase, hoping the Lord will guide to what is nearer than this to right conduct.

studies.applyIt: Take a decision you are close to making and add one sentence to it before you decide: that you could get this wrong and would like to be guided. Say it as a request, not a formality. This ayah puts the plea in the middle of good reasoning rather than in place of it, which is where most of us leave it out.

studies.title: When The Sun Went Down
studies.meaning: The sequence ends here. Abraham has watched a star, then the moon, then the sun, each time calling it his lord and then withdrawing when it set. Early scholars differ over whether he was reasoning his own way towards God or arguing with his people by adopting their premise and following it to collapse. Either way the conclusion is not that the sun is small, but that whatever sets cannot be what he is looking for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is largely an argument with people who worshipped God alongside other powers. Abraham is brought in as the ancestor they claimed. Early scholars note the strategic point. Mecca traced its line and its sanctuary back to him, and here he is shown rejecting the very arrangement his descendants had settled into. No particular occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: A word for something bursting into view, used of dawn and of blood from a wound. It gives the sun's appearance a suddenness that makes its later setting all the more pointed.
A legal term for being clear of a liability or a charge. Using it here makes the break formal rather than emotional, the way a man publicly renounces a debt he will not carry.
One who turns from the surrounding practice towards what is upright. The Quran uses it repeatedly of Abraham, and it describes a direction taken rather than a doctrine held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Star religion was familiar across Arabia and nearby lands. Some tribes were linked with certain heavenly bodies. Caravans steered by the same stars they called on. Anyone travelling at night knew the order of risings and settings by heart. Abraham's argument works because his hearers were expert watchers. They knew better than anyone that everything in that sky goes down.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage is one of very few places in the Quran that lays out a line of reasoning step by step. The conclusion is reached at the end rather than announced at the start. The classical scholars disagree about what it records. Some read it as Abraham's own search, others as a method of debate. Major authorities have held both readings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test applied is disappearance. Whatever cannot stay is ruled out. That test is open to anyone with patience and a horizon. It needs no text and no teacher. The passage also models a public break with inherited practice, which is costly in any society built on lineage. The declaration at the end is about direction, a face turned, rather than about agreeing to a statement.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier steps of the same sequence, the star and then the moon.
Tells the other Abraham story, the broken idols and the question put to his people.
Shows him arguing about a lord who gives life, with the sun brought into it again.

studies.applyIt: Take something you rely on for a sense of stability: a job, one person's approval, a number in an account. Ask what happens to your footing if it goes, and answer honestly rather than bravely. Abraham's test was not contempt for what he was watching. It was noticing what those things do at the end of the day.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham watched a star, then the moon, then the sun. Each one rose and then went down again. So he told his people that none of them could be his lord. He turned instead to the one who made the sky and the earth.

studies.title: My Lord Encompasses All Things
studies.meaning: The argument is answered rather than continued. He asks why they dispute with him about God when he has been guided, which relocates the disagreement: he is not offering a theory to be weighed against theirs. Then the threat behind their argument is addressed. He does not fear what they associate, and the only exception is what his Lord wills, so even his safety is not claimed as his own. The reason follows: his Lord's knowledge takes in everything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the exchange fits a specific pressure the early community knew. Warnings that abandoned gods would take revenge were part of how households kept members in line, and the sources describe converts being told they would be struck with illness or misfortune. Abraham's answer here addresses that argument rather than an intellectual one, which is why it turns on fear.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a proof or argument, in a form meaning to trade arguments back and forth. It names the activity rather than the content, which is what he is declining to continue.
A verb for containing something with room to spare, used of a vessel large enough for what is poured in. Applied to knowledge, it says nothing overflows or falls outside.
A form of remembering that means retrieving what is already held rather than learning something new. The question assumes his listeners possess what they need and are not consulting it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of offended local powers was practical, not abstract. A tribe attributed a drought, a stillbirth or a lost caravan to a shrine neglected or an oath broken, and such reasoning governed real decisions about where to travel and what to sacrifice. Telling a family you had abandoned their god was, to them, an announcement that you had put the household in danger.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for encompassing gives the name of the widest ayah of the Quran, the one about the seat that extends over the heavens and the earth. The same root also produces the Arabic word for spaciousness and for being at ease, so knowledge and roominess share a set of letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together that are easily separated. He denies fearing what they worship, and immediately qualifies it so that even his fearlessness is not independence. Nothing is being claimed for himself. The passage also treats guidance as a change in standing rather than in opinion, which is why a debate is no longer the right shape for the conversation. He is not defending a position; he is reporting one he was given.

crossReferences.why: Records another dispute with Abraham about his Lord, and how the argument was closed.
Puts the same challenge to his people about worshipping what neither benefits nor harms them.
Uses nearly identical wording about a Lord whose knowledge encompasses everything there is.

studies.applyIt: Notice an argument you keep re-entering with someone who has no intention of moving. Ask what you are actually defending, and whether continuing serves it. You can leave a dispute without leaving the person or the position. This ayah's speaker states his ground, gives his reason, asks one question, and stops there.

studies.title: Which Side Deserves Security
studies.meaning: The argument is turned around. Abraham is being threatened with the anger of the gods. He answers by asking who should be afraid of whom. His opponents had attached partners to God with no warrant sent down for it. The question about which party has more right to safety is left for them to answer. The next verse supplies it. The condition attached, faith not clouded by wrongdoing, is what early scholars discuss most.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing Abraham's dispute with his people right after he disowned what they worshipped. The surah around it applies the exchange to its own audience. They had warned the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that their gods might strike him. Classical sources keep reports of early listeners troubled by the second verse. They took the word for wrongdoing in its widest sense.

keyTerms.note: A word for a sanction or proof that gives someone the right to act, and later for a ruler. Its use here demands documentation: the practice is challenged for having nothing issued behind it.
From the same root as faith and trust. The word for being safe and the word for believing come from one source, which is why the verse can move between them without changing subject.
A verb for clothing something or covering it over, used of confusing truth with falsehood. Faith is pictured as a garment that can be worn with something else layered on top of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of offending a tribal god was practical, not theoretical. Shrines were credited with causing illness, drought or a failed journey when slighted. People arranged their travel and their oaths around that. Threatening someone with a god's displeasure was a real threat in that world. Abraham's reply does not deny that the fear is reasonable. It asks which of the two positions is actually exposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for security shares its root with the word for faith. The two stand in the same sentence at the close of the passage. Arabic lets the verse make its point through sound as well as sense. A listener hears the link between believing and being safe before the argument has been spelled out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Safety is presented as a result of what is true. It is not a result of what is powerful. The question about which party has more right to it assumes that security follows accuracy. A person lined up with reality stands differently from one who is not. That holds whoever happens to be frightened at the moment. The qualifying clause then keeps this from turning smug. Faith is described as something that can be clouded over.

crossReferences.why: Names associating partners with God as a great wrong, the reading given to this passage.
Precedes the argument, where his people dispute with him and he refuses to fear.
Describes God as the ally of believers, bringing them out of darkness into light.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are quietly afraid of that has been shaping your decisions this month. Then ask Abraham's question about it: what is it actually able to do, and on what authority. You are not talking yourself out of the fear. You are checking whether it has the standing you have been giving it.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asks his people why he should fear their gods, when they are not afraid of setting up gods beside God with no proof at all. He asks which side is really safe. The answer is those who believe and do no wrong.

studies.title: That Was Our Argument
studies.meaning: The whole sequence is named and attributed. The reasoning Abraham used was given to him, which commentators take as covering the seeing described earlier and the words he spoke. Then a general statement widens it: God raises in degrees whom He wills. The two names that close the ayah keep the raising from looking arbitrary, since it is done by one who is wise and informed. What looked like a private intellectual achievement is reassigned without being diminished.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the Abraham sequence before the surah turns to the line of prophets that followed him. The story has been used to answer people who argued that their inherited religion needed no justification. This concluding ayah addresses the listeners directly by shifting to your Lord, which draws the argument out of the past and lays it in front of the audience.

keyTerms.note: A word for a decisive case in a dispute, the kind that ends it. Its assignment to God rather than to Abraham is the point of the sentence, since the reasoning was received and not devised.
Steps of a stair, used for gradations of standing. The plural and its indefinite form leave both the number and the measure unspecified, so no scale of ranking is offered to the reader.

From a root for restraining and for sound judgement, the same one that gives the word for a bridle. Wisdom in Arabic includes holding back, which is why it pairs naturally with knowledge of everything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Skill in argument was prized and taught. A man who could carry a case before an assembly protected his family's interests, and the vocabulary of proof and rebuttal was familiar to anyone who had watched a dispute settled in public. Attributing a winning argument to someone else was unusual in that culture, where a good case was a personal credit like a good poem.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about raising in degrees appears elsewhere in the Quran attached specifically to knowledge, in a passage that adds that above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more. The same phrase therefore serves twice, once for a prophet's reasoning and once for the ordinary hierarchy of learning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Insight is presented as given rather than achieved, which unsettles a natural pride. The sequence with the star, moon and sun reads like a mind working, and this ayah says the working itself was a gift. That does not make the effort unreal. It reframes what a person can take credit for, and the closing names guard the reframing from becoming arbitrary, since raising is done knowingly and with judgement rather than by preference.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause about raising in degrees and adds that every knower has one above him.
States the same thing plainly, that Abraham's soundness of judgement was given to him beforehand.
Applies the raising in degrees to believers and to those who have been given knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good idea you had recently and try to trace where it actually came from: a conversation, a book, a mood, a night's sleep. You will not find a clean origin. Sitting with that for a minute is the exercise this ayah proposes, and it makes the credit harder to hold and easier to carry.

studies.title: Each Of Them We Guided
studies.meaning: A list begins, and its ordering is not chronological. Isaac and Jacob are given first as a gift to Abraham, then Noah is mentioned as earlier, then a run of names described as from his descendants. Commentators discuss whether the pronoun refers to Abraham or to Noah, and both readings are old and defensible. The refrain does the work: each of them We guided, repeated so that the achievement in every case is attributed the same way, and the closing line names them as those who do good.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the Abraham sequence and addressed to a city that valued lineage above almost everything. Mecca's leading families traced descent from Abraham through Ishmael and used it as a claim to standing. The list here runs through the same ancestry and measures it by guidance rather than by blood, which quietly changes what an inheritance is.

keyTerms.note: A verb for giving without payment or return, the root behind the Arabic for a gift. It is used through the Quran for children in particular, which places offspring outside anything earned.
A collective noun for what issues from someone, connected by the lexicographers to scattering seed. It covers a line rather than a generation, which is what lets one word carry the whole list.
From a root for beauty and excellence, so the word means doing something well rather than merely doing it. Naming the prophets by this term measures them by quality of action, not by rank.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was the memory system of Arabia. Men could recite ancestry back many generations, and disputes over precedence were settled by who could name a longer or better line. Poets were paid to preserve it. A list of names carrying weight was therefore a familiar genre to this audience, and they would have heard this one as a claim about who the real ancestors are.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the two after it name seventeen prophets in a single sustained run, the longest such list anywhere in the Quran. The order is neither chronological nor alphabetical, and classical commentators noted that it groups figures by kinship and by kind, placing relatives beside one another rather than following the centuries.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is stated as the common factor across an immensely varied set of lives, which include a king, a fugitive, a prisoner and a man who preached for centuries. Nothing else in the list is shared. That makes the repeated refrain the actual claim of the passage: what these people had in common was not their circumstances or their success but the same thing being given to each of them.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same gift to Abraham of Isaac and, in addition, Jacob, each made upright.
Places prophethood and the Book within his descendants, which is what this list then traces.
Gives a parallel list of those to whom revelation was sent, overlapping with this one substantially.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the names in this list you know least about and read a short account of that prophet this week. Most readers have three or four they know well and the rest as names. Filling in one changes how the list reads, because it stops being a recitation and starts being people whose lives went differently.

studies.title: Their Fathers And Their Brothers
studies.meaning: The list continues and then, in the final ayah, opens outward in three directions at once: their ancestors, their descendants, and their brothers. Commentators note that this closing phrase deliberately refuses to draw a line around the group. Not every relative is included, since the word used means some of them, and not only sons are named. The passage ends with two verbs, chosen and guided, which describe what was done rather than who deserved it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and part of the longest sequence of prophetic names in the Quran. The audience included people from the scriptural communities of the region as well as Meccans, and several of these names belonged to traditions the Meccans knew only indirectly. Naming them together in one breath asserts a single line of guidance behind traditions the region had come to treat as separate.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be fit or in good working order, used of a repaired wall or a workable arrangement. Uprightness in Arabic is soundness rather than sanctity, which keeps the word ordinary.

An intensive verb from the root for surplus and what remains over. Favour here is described as something extra given rather than a merit recognised, which fits a passage where everything is attributed.
A verb for gathering something up and selecting it out, used of collecting the best of a crop. It implies picking from among many rather than finding the only candidate available.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian families were extended and layered: brothers, half-brothers, cousins raised as siblings, and adopted members who took the family name. A household's identity was collective, and honour or shame travelled through all of it. Against that background, saying that only some of the fathers, descendants and brothers were chosen makes an unusual claim in a society where lineage carried the whole family together.
studies.didYouKnow: The list places related figures side by side rather than following the centuries. Moses and Aaron close the previous ayah as brothers, and this one opens with Zechariah followed immediately by John, a father and his son. The final ayah then makes the principle explicit by naming ancestors, descendants and brothers together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates lineage from selection while running them along the same lines. Prophethood is repeatedly given within families, and it is never given to a family as such. That distinction protects two things at once: the reality of inherited faith, which the Quran treats as a genuine advantage, and the fact that it confers nothing automatically. Being related to guidance is not the same as receiving it.

crossReferences.why: Names families chosen above the worlds, describing them as descendants issuing one from another.
Gathers many of these same figures as those God favoured, from several distinct lines of descent.
States that prophethood was placed in the descendants of Noah and Abraham, with mixed results.

studies.applyIt: Think of the faith you inherited from your family and name one thing in it that came to you already made, that you have never had to build. It might be a habit of prayer or simply the assumption that God is there. Say what it is, and thank whoever passed it down, aloud if they are still reachable.

studies.title: Such Is God's Guidance
studies.meaning: The long list is summarised in three words and then given a condition. All of that was God's guidance, given to whom He wills among His servants, and the second half states what would have undone it. Had even these figures associated others with God, their work would have collapsed. Commentators note the force of applying that clause to prophets. The point is not a warning aimed at them but a statement that nothing in the list was secured by the standing of the people in it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a passage that ran through the whole prophetic line. The Meccans acknowledged a supreme God and added others alongside Him, and the surah has been arguing that the addition is not a small adjustment. Placing this ayah at the end of the list applies the argument at its strongest point, to the very figures whose authority both sides accepted.

keyTerms.note: A vivid verb, used of an animal that eats bad pasture and swells before dying. Work that comes to nothing is pictured as something that looks full and then fails, rather than something small.
The same word this surah uses of all humanity. Its use here, in a sentence about prophets, quietly keeps them inside the general category rather than raising them out of it.

The verb of willing, left unqualified. The Quran uses it in this construction without stating a criterion, and mainstream commentators read the silence as deliberate rather than as an absence of explanation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grazing was a constant calculation. A herd moved onto rich ground could bloat and die, and the swelling looked at first like the animal thriving. Herdsmen knew the sign and dreaded it, since the loss came exactly when the beast appeared at its best. The verb in this ayah carries that picture, and the audience would have heard it before hearing anything abstract.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for deeds coming to nothing appears more than a dozen times in the Quran and almost always in this construction, about work rendered void. Its literal sense, preserved in the classical dictionaries, is a beast swelling from bad pasture, which gives the moral term a physical picture of ruin disguised as abundance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Everything the passage has described is placed under one condition, and the condition is applied to the most exalted possible subjects. Nothing accumulates a standing that could survive it. That is the surah's central argument reaching its sharpest form: association is not one fault among others but the thing that empties the rest. It also explains why a book so patient about most failings returns to this one so often.

crossReferences.why: States the same condition directly to a messenger, that association would render his work worthless.
Describes what this guidance does, leading those who follow it out of darkness into light.
Shows deeds coming to nothing on the same principle, so that no weight is given them at the reckoning.

studies.applyIt: Look at one good thing you do regularly and ask honestly what else is mixed into it: a reputation, a habit of being seen doing it, an obligation to someone watching. You are not obliged to purify it in an afternoon. Just find the mixture and know it is there. This ayah says the mixture is what matters most.

studies.title: Entrusted To Another People
studies.meaning: Three things are said to have been given: the Book, sound judgement, and prophethood. Then the conditional arrives, and it is not a threat but an observation about how this has always worked. If the people in front of you reject these, they have already been entrusted to others who do not. Commentators note that the sentence is in the past tense, so the alternative is not a plan held in reserve. It has been done already.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the rejection in view is the immediate one, from a city that had heard the recitation for years. The classical commentators differ over who exactly is meant by the people entrusted, some reading it of the emigrants and helpers who would form the community, others more broadly of anyone who receives it in any generation. The reading is left open.

keyTerms.note: From the root for restraining and deciding, covering wisdom in judging a matter. Placed between scripture and prophethood, it names the capacity to apply a text rather than merely to receive it.
From the root for an agent given responsibility for another's affairs, used earlier in this surah when the Prophet is told he is not such an agent over anyone.
A demonstrative for people present and close at hand. Its use makes the sentence concrete: the rejection being discussed belongs to the room, not to a category of humanity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trades and offices passed within families and could be lost. A clan held the keys to the sanctuary, another the right to water pilgrims, and these functions were inherited, argued over and occasionally transferred when a line failed or fell out of favour. Everyone understood that a hereditary charge could move to another house. The ayah uses that familiar mechanism for something much larger.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for entrusting in this ayah comes from the same root as the word used a few pages earlier when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is told he is not a keeper over his people. The same letters therefore mark both the responsibility he is released from and the responsibility given to those who receive the message.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as never being at risk, only its custodians. That relocates the anxiety: the question is not whether the message survives but who is carrying it, and the answer to that has changed before and can change again. The passage also gives a curious comfort to a small and pressured community, since it says the succession does not depend on the people who currently hold the standing.

crossReferences.why: Names the same three gifts, the Book, judgement and prophethood, given to an earlier community.
States the replacement principle plainly: turn away and others will be brought who are not like you.
Describes a people God will bring in place of those who turn back, loved by Him and loving Him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something valuable you are the current holder of: a family practice, a piece of knowledge, a role in a community. Ask who you are handing it to and whether you have started. Nothing in this ayah is about loss of the thing itself. It is about who ends up carrying it, and that is decided by whoever bothers.

studies.title: I Ask You No Reward
studies.meaning: The instruction is to follow their guidance, and commentators are careful about what that means. It is not to copy the particular laws given to earlier communities but to take the same path they were on, since the ayah has just described that path as one thing. Then the address turns to the audience with a disclaimer about payment. Nothing is being charged for this, and the final clause states what it is instead: a reminder, offered to everyone, with no transaction attached.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the disclaimer answers a live suspicion. Religious functions in the city generated income, from custodianship of the sanctuary to fees for divination, and a new claim about God was naturally read as a bid for a share. Several Meccan surahs record the same denial in almost the same words, which suggests the suspicion was persistent rather than occasional.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a model or standard, in a form that means taking someone as a pattern. The final letter is a rare orthographic feature that most reciters preserve, marking the word as a stopping point.
The ordinary word for pay owed for work done, used of a hired labourer. Its plain commercial sense is what makes the denial concrete rather than pious.
Not new information but the retrieval of something already known. Describing the whole message this way limits the claim: what is offered is recollection rather than a novelty being sold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's religious economy was visible. Water rights for pilgrims, custody of the sanctuary and the fairs that surrounded it were sources of income and status held by particular families. Poets and diviners were paid for their services. Anyone speaking about the gods in that city was assumed to be positioning for a portion, which is the assumption this ayah steps around by naming it.
studies.didYouKnow: The denial of asking for payment recurs through the Quran in the mouths of many messengers, including several in earlier stories, always in similar words. In one surah alone it is repeated five times by five different figures. The consistency makes financial disinterest a stated feature of the office rather than a personal virtue.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Removing payment removes a motive, and the passage offers that as evidence rather than as a claim to virtue. If nothing is being collected, the usual explanation for why someone persists is unavailable. Calling the whole message a reminder makes a further point about its content. It claims to recover something people already have rather than to introduce a system, which is why it can be offered to everyone without adjustment.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same two clauses almost word for word: no payment asked, and only a reminder to the worlds.
Gives the one exception ever named: that whoever wishes may take a way toward his Lord.
Puts the identical disclaimer in the mouth of an earlier messenger addressing his own people.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you do for others and check what you are quietly collecting for it: thanks, a reputation, the sense of being the reliable one. Do the same thing this week without any of it reaching you, if you can arrange that. Notice whether you still want to do it. That is the whole experiment this ayah suggests.

studies.title: They Did Not Value God
studies.meaning: The charge is stated as a failure of estimation rather than of belief. Saying that God has revealed nothing to any human being is treated as underrating Him, since it denies Him the ability to speak. The answer is a question with a fact inside it: who sent the Book Moses brought, described as light and guidance. Then the handling of that Book is described, put onto sheets, some shown and much concealed. The instruction that closes it is to say the answer and walk away.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical commentators differ over who is being addressed in the middle of the ayah. Some read the whole ayah as directed at Meccans who denied revelation outright, others as shifting to those who possessed the earlier scripture and handled it selectively. The shift between plural addressees in the Arabic is what produces the disagreement, and the tradition records both readings.

keyTerms.note: A verb for assessing size or worth, used of weighing a load or judging a distance. The failing named is therefore a mismeasurement rather than a denial, which is a subtler and more common error.
The plural of the word used earlier in this surah for a writing sheet, and its only other occurrence in the Quran. Both appearances fall within these ninety ayat.
The noun from the verb for walking into water of unknown depth, used a few ayat earlier in this surah for careless talk about God's signs. Its return here closes a loop.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in that region existed as scrolls kept by communities who could read them, and access ran through the few people able to do so. A text was recited to a gathering by someone who chose the passage. That arrangement was normal and gave real power to the reader, since what was not read aloud effectively did not exist for the people listening.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about not valuing God as He deserves appears three times in the Quran, always in this exact form, and each time it introduces a different failure of estimation. Here it is the denial that God speaks to human beings; elsewhere it precedes descriptions of His power over creation on the day of resurrection.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denying revelation is treated as a claim about God rather than as caution about human claims. To say that nothing has ever been sent down is to describe a God who does not communicate, and the ayah says that this is a diminished picture. The mention of Moses then does the argumentative work, since the Book he brought was acknowledged across the region, and its existence answers the general denial without any appeal to the present case.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about not appraising God with the appraisal He is due.
Describes the same Book brought by Moses in the same terms, containing guidance and light.
Names the covenant to make scripture clear to people and not to conceal any part of it.

studies.applyIt: Consider whether your working picture of God includes His speaking to people. Many of us hold the idea of a creator easily and the idea of address awkwardly. Read one page of the Quran today as something said rather than something written, aloud if you can. The difference is not sentimental; it is what this ayah says was being underrated.

studies.title: The Mother Of Cities
studies.meaning: Four things are said about this Book in one sentence: it was sent down, it is blessed, it confirms what came before it, and it has a purpose, to warn a particular city and what surrounds it. Commentators identify the Mother of Cities as Mecca and discuss how far the surrounding area extends, with answers ranging from the nearby settlements to the whole earth. The last clause identifies who responds, and links belief in the hereafter to a habit rather than to an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the phrase naming the city belongs to that setting: the surah addresses the place where it was being recited. The word for confirming what came before assumes an audience aware of earlier scripture, which the Meccans were, through trade and through the communities on their routes. No occasion is reported for this ayah in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a camel kneeling and settling, giving the idea of good that stays in place. Blessing in Arabic is abundance that has come to rest rather than a burst of it.
A phrase for the settlement from which others derive, the way a mother is the origin of a family. It names Mecca by function rather than by size, since it was not large.

An intensive form of the verb for preserving, the same root that gives the word for the guardians mentioned earlier in this surah. Applied to prayer, it means keeping something rather than performing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small, dry and agriculturally poor, and it mattered because of the sanctuary and the trade routes that met there. Settlements around it depended on the season of pilgrimage and the caravans it organised. Calling it the mother of cities described a relationship of dependence that the region recognised, and that had nothing to do with its population or its wealth.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the city appears only twice in the Quran, here and in a later Meccan surah, and both times in a sentence about warning. The parallel passage adds that the Quran was revealed in Arabic for that purpose, which the classical commentaries read alongside this ayah as its companion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Book is described as continuous with what preceded it rather than as a replacement, which shapes how the earlier scriptures are to be regarded. The final clause makes a quieter point. Belief in the hereafter is linked to guarding the prayer, so a conviction about what comes later shows up as a practice now, and the passage treats the practice as the visible form of the belief rather than as its consequence.

crossReferences.why: Names the same city and the same purpose, warning it and those around it, in an Arabic recitation.
Describes the revelation with the same word for blessed, and asks whether they will deny it.
States the confirming relationship at length, as a criterion over the scriptures that came before.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your prayers are things you perform or things you keep. The verb in this ayah is about guarding something, the way you guard an appointment you would not miss. Pick the prayer most likely to slip this week and protect it in advance, by deciding now where you will be and what will be paused.

studies.title: In The Floods Of Death
studies.meaning: The question about who does greater wrong returns, now with three specific answers: inventing against God, claiming revelation that never came, and offering to produce something like what God sent down. Commentators connect these clauses to men who made such claims in that period, and their identifications differ. Then the scene shifts abruptly to a deathbed, with angels reaching out and a command to give up the soul, and the reason stated in the same breath: what was said about God, and pride before His signs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage about who may speak for God. The claim to produce something comparable was made publicly in the city, and the Quran elsewhere records the challenge to attempt it. The classical sources name different individuals behind the middle clauses and do not agree, so the ayah is best read as describing a category of claim rather than a single person.

keyTerms.note: Water deep enough to cover a person entirely, from a root for submerging. Death is described as a rising level rather than a blow, which matches how dying is usually experienced from inside.
The participle for spreading something open, used of an outstretched hand. Arabic uses the same gesture for giving and for taking, so the image is direct without being explained.
From a root for being light in weight and therefore of little account. The punishment is named by the loss of standing rather than by pain, which answers the pride mentioned at the end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drowning was the specific terror of a people who mostly could not swim and who crossed the Red Sea for trade. Flash floods in the valleys were more familiar still: a dry wadi could fill in minutes after rain somewhere out of sight, and people camped in them died without warning. The word used here for death belongs to that experience of water arriving and rising.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening question of this ayah, asking who does greater wrong, is the same one that opens an earlier ayah in this surah, and the surah uses it more than once. Reading the two together shows the second expanding the first, since one clause about inventing against God becomes three distinct claims about speaking in His name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speaking falsely for God is placed at the extreme end of wrongdoing, and the reason given at the end of the ayah pairs it with pride before the signs. The two belong together: claiming to speak for God and refusing what He has said are both ways of putting the self where revelation should be. The scene at death then removes the possibility of continuing, which is what makes it the natural end of the passage.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical question earlier in this surah, with one clause where this has three.
Gives a parallel scene of angels taking souls, described from outside rather than through the dying.
Records the answer to the third claim: an invitation to produce a single comparable chapter.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you attach God's name to your own preferences in conversation, in phrases that make a personal view sound settled. Everybody does it and mostly without noticing. Once today, catch yourself before the phrase and say the opinion as your own instead. It is a small correction, and this ayah is about the direction it points in.

studies.title: You Have Come Alone
studies.meaning: Three things are named as absent. The company is gone, since each arrives singly as they were first created. The possessions are gone, described as left behind the back, which commentators note is the position of something you are walking away from rather than something taken. And the intercessors are gone, along with the claim that they had a share in you. The last clause states the result as a cutting: whatever ran between you has been severed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and addressed to a society organised entirely around belonging. A person in Arabia was a member before they were an individual, protected by a clan and known by a lineage, and wealth was held and displayed collectively. Describing arrival as singular removed every structure the audience relied on for identity, which is what gives the scene its force rather than any description of punishment.

keyTerms.note: A plural formed from the word for one, so the Arabic says many people each alone. It describes a crowd of individuals rather than solitude, which is a more precise and stranger picture.
An intensive verb for granting property and dependants into someone's charge. The root is connected to livestock and management, so what is given is described as placed in one's keeping.
An intensive form of cutting, suggesting something broken apart at many points rather than divided once. Applied to the link between people and what they relied on, it names a thorough separation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan's standing was countable: camels, dependants, clients, sons. These were displayed at gatherings and recited in poetry, and a man diminished in any of them was diminished absolutely. Even a burial was collective, in the ground of a family. The picture of arriving with none of it, in the state of an infant, contradicted every available way of describing a person.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for individuals arriving one by one is grammatically a plural built on the singular for one, a construction Arabic uses sparingly. It occurs twice in the Quran, and the other occurrence is an instruction to stand for God in pairs and singly, so the same rare form describes both a discipline and a destination.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage strips a person down to what cannot be transferred and says that this is what arrives. Property was given and remains given; the wording never denies that it was real. What it denies is that any of it belongs to the person in the sense they assumed. And by naming the intercessors as absent, the ayah closes the surah's long argument about intermediaries with an image rather than another statement.

crossReferences.why: Uses almost identical words about coming as you were first created, against a claim of an appointment.
States the same singularity: every one of them will come to Him on that day alone.
Names what will not help on that day, neither wealth nor sons, leaving only a sound heart.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and pick the three things you would find hardest to lose. Not people, objects. Say what each one does for you, in a sentence. The ayah describes them being left behind the back rather than confiscated, which is a gentler picture and a more accurate one. Knowing what they carry makes them lighter.

studies.title: Who Splits The Seed
studies.meaning: The picture is agricultural and very small. God is the one who splits the grain and the date stone, which is the moment nobody watches, underground, when a hard closed thing opens. Two reversals follow, the living drawn out of the dead and the dead out of the living, and commentators read these both literally, of seed and egg and corpse, and more broadly. The closing question is not rhetorical decoration. It asks how a person turns away after that.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the beginning of a long run of ayat about the natural world that follows the surah's argument with the deniers. The audience farmed at the oases and lived on dates and grain brought in by caravan. The passage does not argue from anything remote. It starts with the two things most likely to be in a Meccan storeroom.

keyTerms.note: An active participle for splitting something open lengthwise. It is used again in the next ayah for the dawn, so the same action covers a seed cracking and the horizon opening at first light.
The collective noun for cereal grains, the staple of the diet. Pairing it with the date stone covers the two crops the region depended on, one imported by caravan and one grown at the oases.
A passive verb for being diverted from a direction, used of something overturned. The passive form is notable: the question asks what is turning them, not simply why they turn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date stones were everywhere. They were fed to camels, burned as fuel, and pressed into the ground to grow new palms, and a farmer knew that a stone had to be kept damp for weeks before anything happened. Nothing about the process was visible while it worked. The ayah picks the least dramatic event in the agricultural year and makes it the evidence.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for splitting appears again as the first word of the very next ayah, applied to daybreak. The repetition links the smallest scale in the passage to the largest without a connecting phrase, which is a compression Arabic allows and English translations usually have to spell out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument moves through the ordinary rather than the exceptional, which is characteristic of this surah after its long dispute about miracles. Nothing here is a suspension of the usual order; it is the usual order, described accurately. The two reversals also answer the resurrection question sideways, since bringing life from what is dead is already happening in every field, on a schedule everybody plans their year around.

crossReferences.why: States the same two reversals in a prayer, bringing the living from the dead and the reverse.
Puts the identical question to the same audience: who is it that brings the living out of the dead?
Offers dead ground revived and grain brought out of it as a sign, using the same argument.

studies.applyIt: Put a few seeds in damp cotton wool on a windowsill this week, or a date stone in a pot of soil. Look at it once a day. Nothing will happen for a while and then something will. The ayah rests its case on that specific event, and most adults have not actually watched it since childhood.

studies.title: He Splits The Dawn
studies.meaning: Three things are named in one line, and each is given a purpose. Daybreak is described with the verb used a moment earlier for a seed, so first light is an opening rather than an arrival. Night is made for rest, using a word connected to dwelling and tranquillity. The sun and moon are set for calculation, which is the most practical claim in the ayah. Two names close it, and the tradition reads them as pairing power with the precision that makes such an arrangement work.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, continuing a sequence of signs drawn from the natural world. The audience navigated, dated debts, timed pilgrimages and planned caravans by the sun and moon, and did so with real skill. The ayah does not tell them anything they did not know about the sky. It renames what they already used as something arranged deliberately for their use.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun for the coming of morning rather than the word for morning itself. It names the transition, the process of becoming light, which is what the verb for splitting is applied to.
From the root that produced the verb used earlier in this surah for whatever comes to rest in night and day. Night is not merely dark here; it is described as a dwelling place.
A noun from the root for counting and accounting. Applying it to the sun and moon makes their motion a measuring instrument, and the same root gives the word for the final reckoning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab timekeeping was lunar and precise enough to run a trading economy. Debts fell due at named moons, the sacred months when fighting stopped were fixed by the calendar, and the two great caravans left at set seasons. Nobody carried a device. The whole system depended on people looking up, which is why calling the sun and moon a means of reckoning described a working infrastructure.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for reckoning in this ayah also gives the Arabic for arithmetic and for the account rendered on the day of judgement. The same three letters therefore cover the motion of the sun, the sum a merchant does, and the final accounting, which is a link the Quran uses more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assigns purpose to things that would otherwise be brute regularities, and the purposes named are human ones: rest and measurement. That says something specific about the relation between the cosmos and the people in it. The two closing names guard against the arrangement seeming impersonal, since a system of that precision is attributed to one who is described as both irresistible and knowing.

crossReferences.why: Spells out the same purpose, that you may know the count of years and the reckoning by them.
States the sun and moon running by exact calculation, in a surah listing what has been given.
Makes night and day two signs, one erased and one made visible, for the same practical ends.

studies.applyIt: Get up once this week in time to watch the sky change before sunrise, and stay with it from grey to colour. It takes about twenty minutes. The ayah calls this a splitting, and the word only makes sense if you have seen the whole process rather than the finished result on your way somewhere.

studies.title: Guided By The Stars
studies.meaning: A single purpose is given for the stars, and it is navigational: so that you may find your way by them in the darknesses of land and sea. The plural for darkness returns from earlier in the surah, and so does the pairing of land and sea. Commentators note the modesty of the claim. Nothing is said about the stars' influence or their meaning, which was the common assumption of the region. They are described as markers, and the ayah closes by naming who reads such a sign.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a run of ayat about the natural world addressed to people who knew the sky professionally. Astral religion existed across the ancient Near East and had left traces in Arabian practice, and the sequence about Abraham earlier in this surah addresses it directly. Here the stars are given a use rather than a status, which is itself the argument.
