keyTerms.note: The plural of a word whose root means to appear or rise. The same root gives the verb for something occurring in due course, so a star is named by its arrival on schedule rather than by its brightness.

keyTerms.gloss: that you may find your way
keyTerms.note: The same verb used through the Quran for being rightly guided. Applying it to navigation lets the physical and the moral senses stand in one sentence without a comparison being made explicit.

keyTerms.gloss: We have set out in detail
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for separating something into distinct parts, used of jointing a carcass. It describes explanation as taking a whole apart so the pieces can be seen individually.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert guides were specialists, hired for their memory of stars and terrain, and a good one commanded a high price. They travelled at night in summer to avoid the heat, steering by particular stars whose seasonal positions they had learned as boys. A caravan's survival depended on one man's recall of the sky. This ayah describes their working method and names its origin.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for being guided in this ayah is the ordinary word for finding a road, and the Quran uses the same root for guidance in every religious sense. Arabic has no separate vocabulary for the two, which means every mention of the straight path carries a traveller's meaning underneath it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The stars are demoted and dignified in the same breath. They are not powers to be consulted about a marriage or a journey's fortune, which was the practice of the region, and they are placed there deliberately for people who need to get somewhere. That combination is the surah's method throughout: nature is emptied of rival authority and filled with intention. The closing phrase attaches the reading of it to knowledge.

crossReferences.why: States the same use in fewer words, landmarks on the ground and stars by which people are guided.
Uses the same phrase for the darknesses of land and sea, there as the place where people call out.
Describes the lamps set in the nearest sky, giving them a different assignment in the same register.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and find one star or planet you can identify, and learn its name if you do not know it. Then find it again tomorrow. Two nights is enough to notice it has moved, and to feel why a person would trust it to tell them where north is. That familiarity is what this ayah assumes.

studies.title: From A Single Soul
studies.meaning: Humanity is traced to one origin, and then two words follow that the commentators have read in several ways. One means a place of settling and the other a place of deposit, and the readings offered include the womb and the loins, the earth and the grave, and life and what precedes it. The tradition preserves the range rather than choosing. What the ayah establishes is not the identification but the shape: every person is passing through stages, some settled and some temporary.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside a sequence of signs drawn from creation. The claim of common descent had social force in a society organised by lineage, where a family's worth was argued from ancestry. Placing everyone's origin in one soul cut across that, and the surah has already argued that guidance and standing do not travel through blood.

keyTerms.note: A verb for raising something up and developing it, used of growing a plant or founding a settlement. It implies a process rather than an instant, which suits an ayah about stages.
A noun of place from the verb to settle, used earlier in this surah for where news comes to rest. Here it names a stage where something stays for a period.
From the root for entrusting something to someone's keeping, as goods are left with a custodian. What is deposited is by definition collected later, so the word carries impermanence in itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Deposits were a familiar arrangement. A traveller leaving Mecca left goods, money or a family member with someone trustworthy and collected them on return, and the whole system ran on reputation because nothing was written. Everyone had held something for someone or left something behind. The word in this ayah belongs to that practice, and it names the difference between where you live and where you are being kept.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words at the centre of this ayah are read differently by different classical authorities, and the commentaries list the possibilities side by side without settling them. Such open cases are rarer than readers expect, and this is one of the clearest: the tradition records that the meaning is disputed and leaves it there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Common origin is stated as a fact about creation rather than as an ethical appeal, and the ethics follow anyway. If everyone came from one, the divisions people build are arrangements rather than natures. The stages named add a second point. Some of what a person occupies is a residence and some is storage, and knowing which is which changes how tightly anything is held, including a body.

crossReferences.why: Opens a surah with the same origin from one soul, and draws an obligation about kinship from it.
Repeats the phrase and continues into the making of a mate and the beginning of a family.
Describes the stages further, creation after creation within three layers of darkness.

studies.applyIt: Think of the person you feel most distant from by background: a different country, class, or generation. Hold the thought that they came from the same origin you did, without turning it into a resolution. It is a fact rather than a feeling, and letting it sit for a minute does more than deciding to be tolerant.

studies.title: Watch The Fruit Ripen
studies.meaning: The ayah moves like a camera. Water comes down, then vegetation of every kind, then green shoots, then grain packed in layered clusters, then palms with their fruit hanging low, then vineyards and olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Commentators note that the sequence follows the actual order of growth. Then comes the instruction, and it is the only imperative in the passage: look at the fruit when it forms and when it ripens. Attention is what is being asked for.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the plants named belong to the wider region rather than to the barren valley of Mecca itself. Olives and pomegranates grew in Syria and Yemen, along the routes Meccan traders used, and dates came from the oases. The audience knew all of them as goods and as landscapes seen on the road, which makes the list a description of the world they moved through.

keyTerms.note: A participle for things mounted or stacked in layers, from the root for riding. Applied to grain it describes an ear of wheat exactly, with the seeds overlapping in rows.
A plural for the heavy bunches that hang from a date palm. The adjective attached means near or within reach, which is a farmer's observation about a mature tree bending under its load.
A noun for fruit coming to maturity, used only here in the Quran. Its rarity marks the second half of the instruction, since watching the forming and watching the ripening are named as two acts.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date palm was a household's security. It took years to bear, produced for decades, and its yield was counted, sold forward and used to settle debts. Families knew individual trees. The detail about clusters hanging within reach is not decorative; it describes the moment in the season when a tree is worth what it is worth, and everyone waited for it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for ripening in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The list around it is also unusually specific, naming four crops by name in one sentence, which is more botanical detail than almost any other passage carries. The instruction to look is placed after that specificity rather than before it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage asks for observation rather than assent, which is a distinctive move. Its argument is not that growth is inexplicable but that it is worth watching, and the phrase about fruits similar and dissimilar points at something particular: the same water and the same soil producing different things. Difference emerging from identical conditions is offered as the sign, and the ayah trusts a careful looker to notice it.

crossReferences.why: Makes the point explicit: neighbouring plots watered with one water, and some are made to excel others.
Lists the same crops after rain, naming olives, palms, vines and every kind of fruit.
Issues the same instruction to look, then walks through the growth of food step by step.

studies.applyIt: Find one growing thing you pass regularly, a tree on your street or a plant on a sill, and look at it properly twice this week, a few days apart. Notice what changed. The ayah asks for exactly this and nothing more, and the reason it asks twice is that the change is the part you cannot see in a single glance.

studies.title: Without Any Knowledge
studies.meaning: Two attributions are named and both are undercut in the same clause that reports them. Unseen beings are made partners to God, and the ayah adds that He created them, which settles the matter without argument. Then sons and daughters are invented for Him, and the phrase attached is the sharp one: without any knowledge. Commentators note that this is the ayah's actual charge. The problem is not merely that the claims are wrong but that they were made about something nobody had any way of knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and both practices named were live in Arabia. Unseen beings were treated as powers to be placated, and some Arabian groups described certain deities as daughters of the high God. The surah has been arguing that speaking about God without warrant is among the worst wrongs, and here it names two familiar examples of exactly that.

keyTerms.note: A verb whose basic sense is tearing or boring through something. Used of invention it suggests forcing a hole where none existed, so the claim is described as damage rather than as decoration.
A recurring Quranic phrase for asserting what one has no access to. It names the procedural fault rather than the content, which is why it can be applied to claims that happen to be about God.
A verbal noun from a root for swimming or moving freely, used to declare God far removed from something. It functions as a denial with a gesture of distance built into it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Unseen beings were part of the practical landscape. Travellers seeking safety in an unfamiliar valley would call on its resident power before camping, and illnesses and sudden strokes of luck were attributed to them. None of this came from a text or a teaching. It was inherited practice, passed on without anyone claiming to have found out anything, which is exactly the situation the ayah describes.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for inventing appears in this sense only once in the Quran, and its ordinary meaning elsewhere is to tear or pierce. The classical lexicographers connected the two through the idea of making an opening in what was whole, so a fabricated claim is pictured as a hole cut into something intact.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies the failure as one of method rather than merely of content. Claims about God are being made by people who have no source for them, and the Quran treats that as the root of the error the rest of the surah has been arguing against. It also sets a standard that cuts in every direction, including toward anyone confident about matters they have not been told anything about.

crossReferences.why: Names the same claim of kinship between God and unseen beings, and what those beings themselves know.
Records the attribution of daughters to God alongside what the same people wanted for themselves.
Describes the practice behind the belief: men seeking refuge in unseen beings and adding to their burden.

studies.applyIt: Pick a confident opinion you hold about something unobservable, and trace where it came from. Not to abandon it. Just find out whether it was told to you, worked out, or absorbed. This ayah's charge is about the absence of a source, and most of us have never checked which of our certainties actually have one.

studies.title: How Could He Have A Son
studies.meaning: The answer runs on a single word. God is called the Originator of the heavens and the earth, a term for making without a prior model, and the question follows directly: how could there be a son when there was never a consort. The reasoning is biological on purpose, since offspring presuppose a pair. Commentators note that the ayah does not argue about status or worthiness. It points out that the category being applied belongs to creatures, and then adds that He created everything there is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the claim being answered had more than one source in the region. Arabian practice described some deities as daughters of the high God, and other communities nearby used the language of sonship in their own ways. The ayah answers the shape of the claim rather than any particular version of it, which is why it works from the meaning of the word itself.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to begin something with no prior example, which also gives the Arabic word for an innovation. It names making that has no model, as distinct from shaping existing material.
The feminine of the ordinary word for a companion, used of a spouse. Its plainness is the point: the argument uses a domestic term, not a theological one, to show where the claim comes from.
An interrogative covering both manner and origin. It asks by what route such a thing could be the case, which is a stronger question than simply whether it is true.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Descent was the organising fact of Arabian life. A person was placed by naming a father, and property, protection and marriage all followed from it. Sons secured a line and daughters made alliances. To speak of offspring in that world was to invoke a whole system of pairing, inheritance and continuation, which is the system this ayah quietly holds up against the word being used.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for Originator here appears only twice in the Quran, both times in this exact phrase about the heavens and the earth. Its root later became the standard Arabic term for a novelty or an innovation, so a name for God and a word for something newly introduced share the same three letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument works by showing that the language of offspring belongs inside creation and cannot be lifted out of it. Anything with a child has a partner, a beginning and a line, and each of those is something the surah has already denied. The closing clause finishes the case economically: everything that exists was made by Him, so nothing is available to be related to Him in that way.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same denial at the shortest possible length, including neither begetting nor being begotten.
Uses the identical name for God and continues into the manner of His decreeing something into being.
Answers the claim of a son at length, describing how grave the tradition takes the statement to be.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you picture God using a family model without meaning to: as a father figure, a stern parent, a distant relative. Most people have a default image of that kind. Name yours once today, and hold it beside this ayah's point that the categories are borrowed. You do not need a replacement picture to see that.

studies.title: No Vision Can Grasp Him
studies.meaning: The first verse gathers a long argument into a conclusion. It names God as Lord and maker of everything, and draws worship as the result. The second verse states a limit. Sight does not reach Him, while He reaches sight. Early scholars record a long discussion of what exactly that rules out. The two divine names that close it are unexpected. Not power or majesty, but fineness and expert awareness, words about closeness rather than distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It closes a passage arguing against giving God children and partners. The surah speaks to people who accepted a creator and then hedged that with go-betweens they could see and handle. The verse about vision speaks straight into that. Early scholars read the pairing as an answer to a demand for something visible to worship, not as an abstract statement.

keyTerms.note: The term for an agent entrusted with another's affairs. Applied to God over all things, it makes maintenance rather than mere origination the point: the world is not left running on its own.
A verb for catching up with something and encompassing it, used of a pursuer reaching what he chases. What is denied is comprehension by sight, which is where the classical discussion begins.
From a root for fineness and delicacy. It carries both being too fine to be perceived and being gentle in dealing with small things, and early scholars keep both senses active here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Worship in Mecca was tactile. Idols were washed, dressed, touched for blessing and carried on journeys, and the sanctuary held images a pilgrim could stand in front of. Religion was something done with the hands and the eyes. Telling that audience their sight could not reach the one they should worship removed the ordinary equipment of devotion and left only words and conduct.
studies.didYouKnow: The two names that close the second verse appear together several times in the Quran. Almost always they come in passages about hidden things: a grain inside a rock, a deed nobody saw, a private grief. The pairing joins fineness of perception to gentleness of treatment. That is why translators struggle to render the first with any single English word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage guards worship against its likeliest failure. That failure is not disbelief but shrinking God down. If what is worshipped could be caught by sight, it would be one object among others. It could be handled as one. Denying that, while saying that He catches all sight, reverses the usual relation between the seer and the seen. The closing names then keep the being out of reach from reading as being far away.

crossReferences.why: States that nothing is like Him, closing with names about hearing and seeing.
Records Moses asking to see, and what happened to the mountain instead.
Uses the same name for subtle awareness, asking whether the creator would not know.

studies.applyIt: Notice the picture that appears in your mind when you pray, whatever it is: a direction, a light, a presence somewhere above. Do not try to correct it into nothing. Just let it be inadequate rather than accurate, and carry on. The verse is not asking you to stop imagining; it is telling you what your imagining is not.
studies.explainEasier: God is your Lord, and there is no god but him. He made everything and he looks after everything. Eyes cannot take him in, but he takes in everything the eyes can see.

studies.title: Whoever Sees, Sees For Himself
studies.meaning: The word translated as insights is a plural for the faculty of seeing rather than for what is seen, so what has arrived is the means of perception. Then the consequences are assigned individually and symmetrically: whoever sees, it is for his own soul, and whoever is blind, it is against it. Commentators note that both outcomes stay with the person. Nothing is transferred to anyone else, which is why the ayah closes with the speaker denying that he is a keeper over them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to an audience that had heard the surah's arguments about creation, revelation and accountability. The disclaimer at the end recurs several times in these pages, and the classical sources treat it as characteristic of the Meccan situation, where the message was being delivered to people who could not be compelled and were not being deceived about what was at stake.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for the faculty of discernment rather than for eyesight. What has come is described as the capacity to perceive, not merely as information to be considered.
The plain verb for lacking sight, used through the Quran for a refusal to perceive. Its pairing with a verb of seeing keeps both outcomes in the same register, as two responses to the same light.
The same root used earlier in this surah for the guardians set over a person, and later for guarding the prayer. Denying the role here separates delivering a message from watching over its reception.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Responsibility in Arabia was collective. A clan answered for its members, paid for their offences and collected for their injuries, and a man's actions were his family's business in a practical and financial sense. Against that background, a sentence assigning the outcome of seeing or not seeing to the individual soul described an arrangement the audience had no everyday model for.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for insight in this ayah shares its root with the word used for the sight taken away hypothetically earlier in this same surah. The two occurrences frame the argument: first the question of who could restore sight if it were removed, and now the arrival of a different kind of seeing altogether.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes perception the thing that has been given, which shifts what a revelation is understood to be. It is not primarily a set of statements but a way of seeing that a person can use or decline. The consequences are then kept strictly personal, and the disclaimer at the end protects that. Nobody is being managed toward an outcome, which means the outcome genuinely belongs to whoever reaches it.

crossReferences.why: Describes the recitation itself as insights from the Lord, using the same rare plural.
States the same symmetry: whoever is guided is guided for himself, and whoever strays only against himself.
Repeats the division and closes with the same denial of being a manager over anyone.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of advice you were given that you can now see was right, and remember how long the gap was before you saw it. Then apply the same patience to something you are currently being told and cannot yet see. The ayah says the seeing is yours when it comes, which also means it arrives on your schedule.

studies.title: You Have Been Studying
studies.meaning: An objection is anticipated and then folded into the purpose. The signs are turned in different directions, and one result is that they will say he has been taught, while another is that it becomes clear to people who know. Commentators note that the same variety produces both responses, so the accusation is not a failure of the method but a consequence of it. What follows is an instruction in three parts: follow what is revealed, hold to the single statement about God, and turn away from those who set up partners.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the accusation was specific. The city suggested that the recitation came from human teachers, and the Quran elsewhere records the charge that a particular foreigner was instructing him. The variety and coherence of the material was itself the point of dispute, which is why this ayah names the diversification and the accusation in a single breath.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for turning something in different directions, used three times in this surah of the signs. Each occurrence pairs it with a different outcome among the listeners.

A verb for reading a text repeatedly until it is learned, from the root that gives the word for lessons. The accusation is not of invention but of schooling, which is a different and more plausible charge.
The same verb the surah uses for those who turn from the signs, given here as an instruction. Its return in the imperative makes withdrawal a discipline rather than the fault it names elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Learning in that world meant sitting with someone. A poet trained under a master, a scribe was taught by a scribe, and a man's knowledge was traced to whoever gave it to him. There was no other model. The accusation that he had studied was therefore the most natural explanation available, and naming a teacher was how anyone would have accounted for unusual material.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb behind the accusation in this ayah is the root of the modern Arabic words for lesson, school and student. Early readers of the text differed over how to vowel it, giving readings that shift the sense between you have studied and it has been studied, and the classical commentaries record the variants together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a hostile reading as anticipated rather than as a problem to be solved, which changes how a believer can hold objections. Not every response to revelation is a failure of the revelation. The instruction that follows then draws the practical conclusion, and its order is worth noticing: follow, affirm, and only then withdraw. Disengagement comes last and after something positive has been secured.

crossReferences.why: Names the same accusation of a human teacher and answers it by pointing at the language itself.
Records a fuller version of the charge, that ancient tales were written down and dictated to him.
Uses the same verb for varying the signs and reports that it only increased their aversion.

studies.applyIt: Notice a criticism of your beliefs that you have been carrying as though it were unanswered, and look up how it has actually been addressed. Ten minutes is usually enough to find that it is old. This passage names an objection in the same breath as the thing that provoked it, which is a calmer posture than either ignoring it or fearing it.

studies.title: Not A Manager Over Them
studies.meaning: Three clauses, and each removes something from the messenger's shoulders. Had God willed, they would not have associated anything with Him, which locates the outcome where it belongs. Then two denials follow, that he was made a keeper over them and that he is a manager of their affairs. Commentators read the pair as covering both watching and acting: he is neither responsible for observing their conduct nor authorised to arrange it. Nothing here criticises the effort. It bounds the office.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the ayat around it deal with the pressure of prolonged refusal. The same denial appears more than once in these pages and in other Meccan surahs, which suggests a burden that recurred rather than a single moment of discouragement. No specific occasion is reported. The wording addresses one person while the surrounding passage addresses everyone.

keyTerms.note: One who guards and keeps a record. Denying the role removes the duty of surveillance, which is the half of responsibility that exhausts a person before any action is even taken.
The one entrusted with another's affairs and empowered to act in them. Paired with the previous word, the two denials cover watching over people and deciding for them.
The verb of willing in a conditional that did not happen. The Quran uses this form repeatedly to state what God could have brought about and did not, without explaining the reason for the restraint.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan household ran on delegated authority. A senior man appointed someone to handle a marriage negotiation, a debt or a caravan's cargo, and that agent's decisions bound the family. It was a real office with real liability. Denying it twice, in two different words, told the listener precisely which two burdens were not being placed on him.
studies.didYouKnow: Both words denied here return elsewhere in the Quran as descriptions of God, who is named the Keeper and the one in whom trust is placed. The same terms therefore mark the boundary of a human role and the character of the divine one, which is a pattern the Quran uses more than once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates persuasion from responsibility at the point where they are most easily confused. Someone who cares about another person's belief naturally starts to feel accountable for it, and this ayah says that feeling has no basis. The opening clause is what makes the release possible. If the outcome was never outside God's will, then failing to produce it was never a failure, and the effort keeps its value regardless.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same denial of being a manager, immediately after naming God as keeper over them.
States the same conditional: had He willed, He would have guided all of you together.
Says plainly that God could have guided all people, in a passage about signs that were demanded.

studies.applyIt: Name one person whose choices you feel accountable for and are not. Write the sentence out: I am not the keeper of this. Then decide what you will still do, which is usually to stay present and stop steering. The ayah removes two burdens and leaves the relationship, which is the part most of us drop while carrying the rest.

studies.title: Do Not Revile Their Gods
studies.meaning: The instruction is given with its reason attached, and the reason is about consequence rather than about the truth of anything. Abuse directed at what others call on produces abuse directed at God, out of hostility and without knowledge, so the outcome is worse than the silence. Commentators are clear that the ayah does not soften the surah's argument against idols; it addresses the manner of speech. The passage then widens: every community finds its own conduct appealing, and every one of them returns to be told what it did.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical commentators report an occasion in general terms. As the message pressed harder on the city's gods, the leadership warned that they would speak against God in return. The reports differ in detail and do not name a single incident consistently, but they agree on the situation: an exchange of insults was beginning and this ayah stopped one side of it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for insulting speech specifically, not for disagreement or refutation. The distinction matters, since the surah spends most of its length arguing against exactly what this ayah declines to mock.
From the root for running and for overstepping a limit, which gives the word for an enemy. It names retaliation that goes past its provocation, which is what an exchange of insults reliably does.
The same verb used earlier in this surah of conduct made to look good. Its repetition here, applied to every community without exception, extends the observation to the listener as well.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Verbal attack was a recognised weapon. Poets were employed to satirise rival tribes, and a well-made insult could travel across Arabia and damage a clan's standing for a generation. Exchanges escalated because each side had to answer. Anyone in that culture understood that beginning such a contest meant committing to it, and that the second insult was never the last one.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about every community finding its own deeds appealing uses the same verb the surah applied earlier to those whose hearts had hardened. Placing it here, immediately after an instruction to the believers, turns a description of other people into a general observation that includes the ones being addressed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Restraint is grounded in effect rather than in respect for the beliefs themselves, which is a precise and unsentimental basis. The passage has been dismantling the practice for a hundred ayat and does not retract a word of it. What it establishes is that mockery achieves nothing the argument wants, and that the harm it provokes lands on the name of God. The general clause that follows removes any smugness from the instruction.

crossReferences.why: Describes the manner of calling others: with wisdom, good counsel, and argument in the better way.
Portrays those who answer the ignorant with peace rather than by returning what was said.
States the general principle, that repelling with what is better can turn hostility into closeness.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group whose beliefs you find easy to mock, and notice the joke you already have ready about them. Retire that one joke this week. Not the disagreement, which you may keep in full. Just the line you use to get a laugh, and see what the conversation about them sounds like without it.

studies.title: Their Most Solemn Oaths
studies.meaning: The promise is made with maximum weight, sworn by God with the strongest oaths available, and it concerns a condition: if a sign came, they would believe. Two answers follow. Signs are with God, which removes the transaction from human hands, and then a question is turned on the believers themselves. What makes you think they would believe if one came. Commentators note that the second answer is addressed to the community rather than to the objectors, which is what makes it striking.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the demand for a sign runs through this surah from its opening pages. By this point the audience has heard the request answered several ways. The classical sources describe specific requests made in the city, including for a hill to be moved and for the dead to speak, and the ayat following this one respond to precisely those images.

keyTerms.note: Literally the utmost of their oaths, using a word for exertion and strain. The phrase names an oath sworn to the limit of what a person's word can bear, with nothing stronger available.
The same word used for a verse of the Quran and for a marvel in nature. Its indefinite form here means any sign at all, which is what makes the request both sweeping and unfalsifiable.
From a root for fine awareness, connected to the words for a poet and for hair. It names perception at the edge of noticing, so the question asks what gives the listeners their confidence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the strongest instrument a person had. There were graded forms, and the heaviest involved swearing by God at a sanctuary, which settled disputes that no evidence could. A man who broke such an oath was finished socially. Hearing that oaths of this weight were being sworn in support of a promise nobody intended to keep would have registered as genuinely shocking.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the most solemn oaths appears several times in the Quran and almost always introduces a promise that is not kept. The recurrence is consistent enough that classical readers treated the expression as a signal, marking a commitment made at the highest volume and the lowest reliability.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage turns from the objectors to the believers and questions their optimism, which is unusual and worth sitting with. Hoping that one more piece of evidence will settle someone is a natural and generous instinct, and the ayah declines to encourage it. That is not cynicism about people. It is a statement about what belief actually rests on, and the ayat immediately following spell out how far the point extends.

crossReferences.why: Extends the answer to its limit: angels, the dead speaking, and everything gathered before them.
States the same conclusion, that every sign together would not move those already settled against it.
Records the demand in another form, asking why God does not speak to them or send a sign.

studies.applyIt: Think of a person you keep hoping will change if the right thing happens to them. Notice how much of your energy is spent waiting for that event. Keep the hope and stop the waiting. This ayah gently questions the assumption, not to make you give up on anyone, but to return the effort to what you can actually do.

studies.title: We Turn Their Hearts
studies.meaning: The verb used is one of overturning, the motion of flipping something over repeatedly, and it is applied to hearts and to sight together. Commentators read the clause that follows as the reason: this answers a first refusal rather than preceding it. The word for heart here is not the usual one; it names the organ at its most alive and receptive. What is described, then, is the most sensitive faculty a person has being turned, and them left to wander in it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following directly on the observation that a sign would not settle anything. The passage is explaining why, and it does so in language that has troubled readers in every generation. The classical commentators handle it by reading the whole surah together, where the refusal comes first and is described many times before this consequence is named.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for flipping something over and over, used of turning meat on a fire or hands in regret. The repetition built into the form suggests instability rather than a single reversal.
A different word from the usual one for heart, connected by the lexicographers to burning and to intense feeling. It names the heart at its most alive, which is what makes its turning significant.
A verb for moving without direction, used of an animal straying in open country. It differs from the word for blindness by describing the behaviour rather than the impairment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel that lost its bearings in featureless country did not stand still. It kept walking, confidently and in wide circles, and a herdsman watching from a rise could see what the animal could not. The verb in this ayah belongs to that scene, which is why it names motion rather than paralysis. The wandering looks like purpose from the inside.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for heart used here appears far less often in the Quran than the more common term, and it tends to occur where feeling rather than understanding is at stake, including in the description of a mother's heart emptied of everything. Its use in this ayah is therefore pointed rather than incidental.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah states a consequence in the strongest possible terms and attaches it to a prior refusal in the same sentence, and the mainstream tradition insists on reading the two halves together. What it rules out is any idea that a person can decline something indefinitely and find the capacity to accept it unchanged. Faculties are described as responsive to use, and the responsiveness runs in both directions.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same closing phrase, leaving them to wander blindly in their overstepping.
States the same order of events, that hearts were turned aside after the people had first deviated.
Places the same wandering after misguidance, and says no guide remains for the one left in it.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you once found moving that now does nothing for you: a passage, a place, a form of worship. Rather than concluding it has gone flat, ask what changed in you between then and now. This ayah's claim is about the receiving end, and that end is the one you have access to.

studies.title: Even If The Dead Spoke
studies.meaning: Three impossibilities are granted in a row, each larger than the last: angels sent down, the dead speaking to them, and everything gathered before them face to face. The conclusion is stated flatly. They would still not believe, unless God willed it. Commentators note that the exception is what keeps the sentence from being fatalistic, since the possibility is left open on God's side. The final clause names the condition of most of them, and the word chosen means ignorance rather than error.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and every item in the list was actually requested. The classical sources record demands made in the city for angels to appear, for particular dead men to be raised and questioned, and for other displays. The Quran elsewhere preserves a longer version of the same list. This ayah answers all of them at once rather than one by one.

keyTerms.note: Read in more than one way by the early authorities, giving the sense of things brought face to face or gathered in groups. The commentaries record the variants side by side without preferring one.
The same verb used in this surah for the assembling of people on the last day. Its use here for evidence brought together suggests a preview of that gathering rather than an ordinary display.

From a root covering both lack of knowledge and rashness of temper. Pre-Islamic usage leans toward the second, so the word describes people acting without weighing rather than people lacking information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Consulting the dead was not an alien idea in that region. Diviners claimed contact with unseen beings, and stories circulated of voices heard at graves or in ruins. Asking for a dead ancestor to confirm the message was therefore a request within the audience's imaginative world. It was not a joke, which is why the ayah answers it in the same register as the others.
studies.didYouKnow: One word in this ayah has several accepted early readings, and each produces a slightly different image: evidence brought face to face, or gathered in groups, or acting as a guarantor. The classical commentaries list them together, which is how the tradition preserves a place where the sense was genuinely open.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a ceiling on what evidence can accomplish and then puts a door in it. Nothing available to a person would produce belief on its own, and yet the exception is God's will, which is neither predictable nor closed. That combination removes two temptations at once: despairing of anyone, and imagining that the right demonstration would settle the matter if only it could be arranged.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the fuller list of demands, from a spring in the ground to a house of ornament.
Answers the first item earlier in this surah, explaining what an angel's arrival would settle.
States the same conclusion, that every sign together would not move those already committed.

studies.applyIt: Notice a conversation you keep planning to have, in which you will finally lay out the evidence and be understood. Most of us have one running. Ask whether more evidence is really what is missing. If it is not, spend that energy on the relationship instead, which is the only part that was ever yours.

studies.title: An Enemy For Every Prophet
studies.meaning: Opposition is described as standard equipment rather than as a misfortune. Every prophet is assigned an enemy, and the enemies are of two kinds, human and unseen, working by the same method: passing gilded speech to one another to deceive. Commentators note that the word for their exchange is the same one used for revelation, which sets a deliberate parallel. The ayah then removes any sense of an evenly matched contest, and closes with an instruction to leave them to it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the reassurance is aimed at a community that had begun to take organised opposition personally. The surah has already placed the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) inside a line of messengers who were denied and mocked. This ayah goes further and describes the opposition itself as part of the arrangement, which reframes it from a setback into a feature.

keyTerms.note: The first word names gold ornament applied to a surface. Speech described this way is not false in a way you can hear; it is plated, attractive on the outside and something else underneath.

The same verb used for revelation given to prophets, in its basic sense of swift concealed communication. Using it of the opposition draws an exact and uncomfortable parallel between two kinds of quiet transmission.
From the root used earlier in this surah for being taken in by the present life. It names the effect rather than the intention, so the word describes what the speech produces in a listener.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gilding was a known craft. Wood or base metal was covered in a thin layer of gold to make an object look solid, and everyone who had traded in the northern markets knew the difference between plated goods and the real weight. Applying that word to speech named a familiar commercial deceit and moved it into the assembly, where reputations were made by phrasing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for gilding in this ayah gives its name to surah 43, where it appears in a passage about the ornament of the present life. The same root therefore titles a whole surah about being impressed by surfaces, which is exactly the mechanism described here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Opposition is given a place in the design, which changes how it is to be read. Its presence is not evidence that something has gone wrong, and its absence would not be evidence that something is right. The clause about God's will keeps the two sides from being equal powers, and the closing instruction is the practical conclusion: attention spent on refuting fabrications is attention not spent on the work.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle almost word for word, an enemy assigned from the criminals to every prophet.
Describes a companion assigned to the one who turns from the reminder, using a related mechanism.
Names companions who make what lies before and behind a person look attractive to him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you were persuaded by mainly because it was said well: an advertisement, a confident speaker, a beautifully written argument. Trace what the actual claim was underneath the phrasing. This ayah's image is plating over base metal, and the test for plating is weight rather than shine.

studies.title: Hearts That Lean Toward It
studies.meaning: The ayah continues the previous sentence and states what the gilded speech accomplishes. Hearts lean toward it, then become pleased with it, then go on to earn what they earn. Commentators note the three-stage sequence: an inclination, then consent, then conduct. The people described are identified by one thing only, that they do not believe in the hereafter, which the passage treats as the condition that makes such speech attractive in the first place.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and belief in an afterlife was the sharpest point of disagreement in the city. Arabian religion accommodated many gods and very little accountability, and the surah has recorded the denial in the objectors' own words earlier. This ayah explains what follows from that denial, describing not an argument but an appetite for a certain kind of talk.

keyTerms.note: A verb for tilting toward something to listen, used of an ear turned to catch a sound. It names a small physical movement rather than agreement, which is why it comes first in the sequence.
The verb of contentment and approval. Its placement second turns the sequence into a description of how a position becomes comfortable: first you lean in, and only afterwards do you accept it.
From a root for gathering fruit or bark by hand. It describes wrongdoing as something collected deliberately, which distinguishes it from a slip and matches an ayah about a gradual process.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Mecca was made and destroyed by talk, and people chose whose talk to sit near. A young man attached himself to a circle, learned its phrases, and within a season held its opinions as his own. Nobody decided to change their mind. The sequence in this ayah, from leaning in to being at ease, describes something the audience had watched happen to their sons.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for inclining used here appears only twice in the Quran, and the other occurrence describes hearts that have deviated. Both times it names a tilt rather than a decision, which fits a vocabulary that treats belief and its loss as gradual movements more often than as sudden reversals.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage traces a mechanism rather than issuing a verdict, and the mechanism is one anybody can recognise. What you listen to becomes what you accept, and what you accept becomes what you do. Placing disbelief in the hereafter at the head of the chain also makes a claim about motive: the question of whether anything follows this life is what decides how much a person can afford to be persuaded of.

crossReferences.why: Describes buying diverting talk in order to lead others from the way, without any knowledge.
Names the residue such conduct leaves, a stain settling over the heart from what was earned.
Gives the counter-instruction: do not pursue what you have no knowledge of, since each faculty is asked.

studies.applyIt: Look at what you listen to most in a week, whatever plays while you drive or cook. Not to judge it. Just notice which opinions in you arrived that way rather than by thinking. The ayah's first stage is only a tilt of the head, and the tilt is the part you can still feel happening.

studies.title: Shall I Seek Another Judge
studies.meaning: The question refuses a procedure rather than an answer. Seeking a judge other than God would mean submitting the matter to an authority above the one who sent the Book, and the Book is described as already set out in detail, so the case has been stated. Commentators note the appeal that follows, to people who possess earlier scripture and recognise what this is. The closing instruction is short and personal: do not be among those who waver.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and arbitration was the standard way of settling a serious dispute in Arabia. Parties agreed on a respected third person and accepted the outcome. The Meccans had proposed such arrangements over other quarrels, and the surah has already refused several offers of compromise. This ayah answers the underlying assumption that the matter was negotiable at all.

keyTerms.note: Specifically the arbitrator both sides agree to, not an appointed magistrate. The word names a role that only exists by mutual consent, which is what makes seeking one here a category error.
From the verb for separating something into its parts, used earlier in this surah for explaining the signs. It describes a text laid out clearly rather than one requiring an interpreter's key.
From a root meaning to dispute back and forth, and connected to milking, drawing something out repeatedly. Doubt in this word is an activity rather than a state, something a person keeps doing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arbitration was a familiar craft with recognised practitioners. Before the message began, the tribes of Mecca had submitted a dispute over rebuilding the sanctuary to the judgement of whoever next entered by a particular gate, and accepted the result. Everyone understood that agreeing on a judge was the first and hardest step, and that the choice usually decided the case.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for arbiter here comes from the same root as the word for wisdom and for the bridle placed on a horse. Arabic connects judging with restraining, so a judge in this vocabulary is one who holds a dispute in check rather than one who wins it for a side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the disagreement outside the reach of negotiation, which is a hard thing to say gracefully and is said here in a question. It also draws a connection between clarity and finality: a text set out in detail leaves less room for the professional mediator. And the closing instruction, addressed to the one carrying the message, treats steadiness as something asked for rather than assumed.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same Book with the same word, its verses set out in detail for people who know.
Names both stages of the text, verses made firm and then detailed, from one who is wise and aware.
Makes accepting God's judgement in a dispute the measure of belief rather than an optional step.

studies.applyIt: Notice a matter you have settled in principle and keep reopening in your head, looking for a second opinion that agrees with you. Everybody has one. Name it, and decide today whether you are actually reconsidering or just shopping. This ayah's word for doubt describes a repeated action, which means it can simply be stopped.

studies.title: Complete In Truth And Justice
studies.meaning: Two qualities are named as the completion of God's word, and the pairing is precise. Truth covers what the word reports and justice covers what it requires, so statements and commands are each accounted for. Commentators read completion here as fulfilment rather than as a stopping point, and they differ over whether the word means the Quran, God's promise, or His decree generally. Then the guarantee: nothing alters His words. The two names at the end tie the promise to attention.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and placed after a passage about seeking arbitration elsewhere. The surah has been arguing with people who kept looking for another authority, another sign, another intermediary. This ayah closes that line by describing the word already given as complete in both directions, leaving nothing outstanding that a different source could supply.

keyTerms.note: A verb for reaching fullness, used of a moon becoming full or a term running its course. It names arrival at wholeness rather than the end of a process of adding.
Truth specifically in speech, the correspondence between what is said and what is so. Pairing it with justice divides the word into what it tells and what it asks, covering both at once.
An active participle in a construction of absolute denial, so the sentence says no such agent exists at all. The same phrase appears earlier in this surah, where it grounds a promise of help.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Agreements in Arabia were oral and were held by memory and witness. A contract could be quietly reshaped over years as the people who heard it died, and disputes about what had actually been said were common. Written treaties were kept in the sanctuary partly for this reason. A word that nobody can alter described exactly the security that oral undertakings lacked.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about nothing altering God's words appears twice in this surah, once earlier as the ground of a promise that help would come to messengers, and once here about the word's completion. The same phrase therefore does two jobs, securing a promise for the future and a text in the present.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth and justice are joined as two aspects of one word, which resists a common separation between what is believed and what is practised. A description that is accurate and a requirement that is fair are presented as the same completion. The unalterability that follows is then not a claim about manuscripts but about the word itself, which is why the two names of hearing and knowing close the sentence.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same clause earlier in this surah, grounding the promise that help reached earlier messengers.
Repeats the guarantee in a passage about the friends of God, as the great attainment.
States it from God's own speech, that the word is not changed with Him, and none is wronged.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise you made that has quietly changed shape since you made it, adjusted by circumstances until it means something easier. Find the original wording, if you can remember it. This ayah's claim is about a word that stays as it was said, and holding one of your own to that standard is a day's work.

studies.title: If You Obeyed Most People
studies.meaning: A count is not an argument. Following the majority of those on earth is described as leading away from God's path, and the reason given is not that they are wicked but that they are guessing. Two words carry it: they follow only conjecture, and they do nothing but estimate. Commentators note that the second word is drawn from guessing at quantity, the trader's approximation of a crop still on the tree. What is criticised is a method, and the method is unexamined consensus.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the community hearing this was very small, surrounded by a city that agreed with itself. Consensus was more than social pressure in Arabia; inherited practice was the basis of authority, and the standard argument against the message was that the ancestors had done otherwise. This ayah answers the form of that argument rather than any particular version of it.

keyTerms.note: A word covering everything from a strong impression to a bare guess. The Quran uses it for belief held without grounds, and the objection here is to the grounds rather than to the content.
A specific term for assessing a crop by eye before harvest, in order to set a price. It names skilled approximation, which makes the criticism sharper: this is guessing that looks like expertise.
The causative of the verb for losing a road, used through this surah. Following is described as being led, so the fault is located in the act of following rather than only in the leaders.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Date crops were valued before picking. An assessor walked the grove, looked at the trees, and named a figure that both parties then treated as the yield for the purposes of a sale or a debt. He was often close and sometimes badly wrong, and nobody found out until the harvest. That practice gives this ayah its verb for conjecture dressed as knowledge.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for estimating in this ayah is a technical term from agriculture, and it survives in Arabic legal vocabulary for assessing standing crops. Its appearance in a passage about belief moves a specialist word from the grove into an argument about evidence, which is a favourite manoeuvre of the Quran's Meccan style.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates truth from popularity without treating the majority as malicious, which is a fairer and more useful criticism. People are described as approximating, which is what people mostly do, and the danger named is inheriting those approximations as though they were findings. That leaves the reader with a specific task rather than a suspicion, which is to ask of any settled opinion how it was arrived at.

crossReferences.why: States the principle plainly: most follow conjecture, and conjecture avails nothing against truth.
Applies the same point to a specific claim, that conjecture is no substitute for knowledge.
Notes the numbers honestly, that most people will not believe however eager you may be.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you believe because everyone around you does, and try to say what the evidence for it is in two sentences. Not to abandon it if you cannot. Most of what any of us holds arrived this way. The exercise is to find out which of your convictions you have actually inspected.

studies.title: Over Which His Name Was Spoken
studies.meaning: The first ayah closes the previous argument by returning the assessment of who is astray to God, which removes the reader from the business of ranking anybody. The second turns to something ordinary: eating from what God's name was pronounced over. Commentators note the condition attached, if you believe in His signs, which ties an everyday act to a conviction. The point of the naming, as the tradition reads it, is acknowledgement of where the animal and the permission came from.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the practice being described existed before the message. Arabs pronounced names over animals at slaughter, sometimes the name of a deity and sometimes of a shrine, and the custom carried real meaning about whose the animal was. The surah's closing section addresses several such practices, and this passage begins that turn from argument toward the details of ordinary life.

keyTerms.note: The passive of the verb for remembering and for saying aloud. One root covers holding something in mind and speaking it, so pronouncing a name is described as an act of remembrance.
A name spoken over something in Arabian practice marked whose it was and under whose protection it fell. The phrase therefore carries ownership and acknowledgement rather than a formula's efficacy.

The same participle used earlier in this surah, in a sentence where the speaker says he would not be among them if he yielded. Its reappearance keeps the category consistently outside human assessment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat was uncommon and its slaughter was public. An animal killed for a guest, a wedding or a season of plenty was an event, and what was said over it was heard by everyone present. The words identified whose the occasion was and who was being honoured. In a society that ate meat rarely, nobody treated the moment as routine.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for mentioning in these ayat is the same one that gives the Quranic term for remembrance of God, and the word used for the Quran itself as a reminder. Speaking a name and holding something in mind are one act in Arabic, which is why the tradition treats invocation as a form of memory.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage moves from a large argument about guidance to a small daily act without changing register, which is characteristic of this surah. Belief in the signs is made visible in what is said over a meal, so conviction is shown reaching into the most ordinary transaction a household makes. And the first ayah keeps the sorting of people where it belongs, which prevents the practice from becoming a badge.

crossReferences.why: Explains why every community was given a rite: that God's name be mentioned over what was provided.
Repeats the same instruction about mentioning the name, and joins it to feeding the poor.
Uses the same phrase in a Medinan setting, alongside the reminder to be mindful of God.

studies.applyIt: Say God's name once before your next meal, out loud, and notice how the first mouthful lands differently. That is the whole exercise. These ayat tie a conviction to a small spoken act at the point where a person is least likely to be thinking about anything, which is exactly when the naming does its work.

studies.title: He Has Set It Out
studies.meaning: The question pushes back against an unnecessary strictness. What has been withheld is described as already detailed, so the list is finite and known, and an exception is named for genuine compulsion. Commentators read the whole passage as answering people who were adding restrictions of their own. The second half identifies where such additions come from: many lead others astray by their inclinations, without knowledge. The closing clause returns the assessment of who oversteps to God.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and Arabian practice included an elaborate set of self-imposed food restrictions attached to particular animals and occasions. The surah names several of them a few ayat later. The commentators describe the objectors arguing directly with the believers about these customs, which is why this passage answers a dispute about food rather than opening one.

keyTerms.gloss: He has set out in detail
keyTerms.note: The same verb used through this surah for separating something into distinct parts. Applied to what is withheld, it implies a definite list rather than an open field of caution.

A passive form from the root for harm and hardship, meaning driven to something by necessity. Its presence keeps the whole subject humane rather than absolute, and the Quran repeats it wherever such limits appear.
The same plural used earlier in this surah when desires were named as what would actually be followed. Its return here says the additions come from appetite, including the appetite for strictness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food rules in pre-Islamic Arabia were local and inherited. Certain animals were set aside after a number of births, some were left to graze untouched after a vow, and particular parts were reserved for men or forbidden to women depending on the tribe. None of it came from a text. It was custom hardened into obligation over generations, enforced by families rather than by any authority.
studies.didYouKnow: The exception for compulsion appears in every Quranic passage that names withheld foods, four times across four different surahs, always in nearly identical wording. That consistency is unusual, and the classical commentaries treat the repetition as deliberate, so that no listing of limits is ever recorded without it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is as concerned with additions as with transgressions, which is a distinctive emphasis. Inventing restrictions is described as leading people astray, using the same verb the surah applies to the deniers, and it is traced to inclination rather than to piety. That leaves an important principle standing: what has been set out is set out, and treating one's own caution as though it came from God is its own kind of speaking without knowledge.

crossReferences.why: Gives the corresponding list with the same exception for one compelled, without desire or excess.
Warns against tongues asserting that this is permitted and that is not, inventing lies about God.
Addresses the opposite error, of declaring unlawful the good things that were made lawful.

studies.applyIt: Notice a rule you keep that nobody gave you: a standard about work, hospitality, or how a home should look. Ask where it came from and whether it is serving anyone. This passage is uneasy about self-imposed restriction dressed as principle, and the first step is simply being able to tell the two apart.

studies.title: Outward Sin And Inward
studies.meaning: Wrongdoing is divided into what shows and what does not, and both are named together in a single short instruction. Commentators read the inward half as covering both hidden acts and the movements of the heart, and they note that Arabic uses the same pairing for the visible and hidden parts of anything. The ayat that follow return to what is eaten and to the arguing that surrounded it, warning that being argued into something has consequences beyond the matter under discussion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the surrounding passage is answering a live dispute about inherited food customs. The classical commentators describe the objectors pressing the believers with arguments framed as reasonable questions, and this passage names that pressure directly. The instruction about sin outward and inward opens the section, giving the specific dispute a wider frame before it is addressed.

keyTerms.note: What is visible on the surface, from the root for a back or an exterior. The word gives the Arabic for something manifest, and it is used across the Quran as one half of a standard pair.
The interior, from the root for a belly. Paired with the previous word it covers a thing completely, so naming both halves of wrongdoing leaves no category of it unaddressed.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for the gilded speech passed between enemies. Its repetition ties the argument about food to the mechanism described a few ayat before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was a full-time occupation in a city where everyone knew everyone. A man's outward conduct was watched constantly, and his standing depended on it, so the difference between what was seen and what was not could be considerable. Naming both halves in one breath addressed a society that had refined the management of the visible half to an art.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of outward and inward in this ayah is the standard Arabic way of saying all of something, the way English says inside and out. The Quran uses the same two words elsewhere of blessings, of the sea and of knowledge, so the phrase here places wrongdoing inside a familiar figure for completeness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the hidden half makes character rather than reputation the subject, and does it without a word about being watched. The passage then draws a line from a small argument about food to something much larger: yielding to pressure in a matter framed as trivial is described as consequential, because what is at stake is not the matter but who is being followed. That is a claim about how allegiance actually shifts.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pairing, naming what is apparent of immoralities and what is concealed of them.
Describes those who avoid the greater wrongs and forgive when they are angry, as a settled quality.
Notes that the ones who avoid the great sins are still known best by the One who formed them.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you do only when nobody can see, and one thing you do only because someone can. Write both down on the same piece of paper. You do not have to act on either today. This passage puts the two halves in one sentence, and seeing them side by side is most of the work.

studies.title: A Light To Walk By
studies.meaning: Two figures are set against each other. One was dead and was given life and a light to walk by among people; the other is in darkness and cannot get out. Commentators note the detail in the first half: the light is for walking among people, not for private illumination, so what was given shows up in company. The second figure is described without a verb of choosing. He is simply in it. The closing clause explains why that condition persists.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical commentators discuss whether the comparison points at particular individuals in the city, with different names offered, or describes two conditions generally. The reports do not agree, and the wording works either way. What is not in dispute is the setting: a community where some had accepted the message and others had refused it, living in the same streets.

keyTerms.note: The causative of living, used through the Quran for reviving dead ground after rain. Applying it to a person makes the change a resurrection in miniature rather than an improvement.
Indefinite and unqualified, so the ayah does not specify what the light is. Commentators offer faith, the Quran and understanding, and the tradition records the range without narrowing it.
An active participle in a negative construction, so the denial is of the person as an emerger rather than of a single exit. The grammar makes the condition a description rather than an event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Walking at night in a town without lighting meant carrying a flame or knowing the ground by memory. A lamp changed everything: you saw the drop, the sleeping animal, the person coming the other way. Those without one waited for dawn or felt their way along walls. Everybody in that audience had done both, and knew which they preferred.
studies.didYouKnow: The light in this ayah is given for walking among people rather than for seeing in the dark alone, and the same phrase appears in a later surah where believers are described walking with their light going before them. The Quran repeatedly attaches this image to movement in company rather than to private illumination.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The change described is not an improvement in someone's opinions but a restoration of life, which sets the stakes higher than persuasion. And the light's purpose is social. What has been received becomes visible in how a person moves among others, which means the difference between the two figures is meant to be noticeable rather than internal. The closing clause keeps the second figure's condition explained rather than merely condemned.

crossReferences.why: Describes God bringing believers out of darkness into light, and the reverse for those who refuse.
Shows the same light in motion, going before believers and to their right on that day.
Draws out the other half of the comparison at length, as darkness layered over darkness at sea.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose presence makes a room easier to be in, and try to name what they actually do. It is usually small and repeatable: they ask, they wait, they do not compete. This ayah describes light as something you walk with among people, which means it is visible in behaviour before it is anything else.

studies.title: The Greatest Of Its Criminals
studies.meaning: An observation is made about how towns are arranged: in each one the leading wrongdoers are its most prominent men. Commentators note the word order, which puts greatness first and criminality second, so the phrase names people who are great in the town's own reckoning. Their activity is scheming. The correction follows immediately and is the ayah's whole point. Whatever they plot lands on themselves, and they do not perceive it, which makes the scheming self-directed without their knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the description fitted the city exactly. Mecca's opposition was led by men of standing, heads of clans with wealth, clients and reputations, and their objections carried weight because of who they were rather than what they said. The ayah generalises that arrangement to every town, which removes any sense that Mecca was unusually bad.

keyTerms.note: A plural for those greatest in a place, by age, wealth or standing. Its position before the word for wrongdoers makes prominence the first thing said about them, which is how the town itself would describe them.
A verb for planning in secret, not necessarily for evil ends, though usually so in the Quran. It names indirect action, working through arrangements rather than through open force.
From the root for fine awareness, the same one behind the word for a poet. Denying it says the effect is real and below the threshold of their noticing, not that they are indifferent to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's power sat with a handful of families who held the sanctuary's offices, financed the caravans, and could make or break a man by withdrawing protection. They met, discussed, and acted together without any formal body existing. The word for scheming describes exactly that: decisions taken among a few people in private that everyone else experienced as circumstances.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the verb for scheming of God as well, in passages where a plot is answered in kind, and the classical commentators discuss the usage carefully. The word itself carries no moral charge in Arabic; it names planning that is concealed, and the surrounding sentence supplies the judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says that harm arranged against others returns to its authors as a matter of how things work, not as an occasional punishment. That is a claim about a moral order built into events rather than imposed on them. The detail about not perceiving it is what makes the ayah unsettling. The mechanism runs whether or not anyone recognises it, so a person can be well into their own ruin and still be reading the situation as success.

crossReferences.why: States the principle directly, that an evil plot encircles none but the people who made it.
Names the same class of people, the affluent of a town, as the ones whose conduct decides its fate.
Shows the two sides afterwards, the followers and the ones they followed, arguing about who misled whom.

studies.applyIt: Think about a small arrangement you have made at work or at home that quietly disadvantages someone, and that you would not describe out loud in those terms. Most of us have one. Say it plainly to yourself. This ayah's warning is not about being caught; it is about a cost that arrives without being noticed.

studies.title: God Knows Where To Place It
studies.meaning: The objection is finally stated in full, and it is about status. They will not believe until they are given what God's messengers were given, which is a demand to be selected rather than addressed. The answer is a single clause: God knows best where He places His message. Commentators note that it does not argue about their qualifications. It relocates the question, since placement is a decision made by the sender, and no candidate is in a position to assess it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the complaint had a concrete form. The classical sources record leading men of the city asking why the message had not come to someone of greater standing in Mecca or in the town to the east, and the Quran preserves that objection elsewhere in almost those words. The claim rested on wealth and clan, which were the city's only measures of importance.

keyTerms.note: A noun for what is sent with a messenger, distinct from the messenger himself. The word treats prophethood as a consignment placed somewhere, which is what makes the verb for placing exact.
From the root for being small in size. It names the reduction of standing rather than pain, which answers precisely what the objectors were asking for, since their demand was about being large.
The comparative of knowing joined to a word for place. The construction is unusual and puts the emphasis on location, so what God knows best is the where of it, not the who.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour in Mecca was measured and displayed. Precedence at a gathering, the right to speak first, the size of a man's following, and the number of guests he could feed were all counted publicly. Being passed over for a distinction was a real injury with financial consequences. The demand recorded here was, in that world, a perfectly conventional grievance about protocol.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for humiliation used at the end of this ayah appears only once in the Quran. It comes from the ordinary root for smallness, and its rarity marks a precise answer: the punishment named for men who demanded greatness is described by the word for being made small.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Selection is placed outside every visible qualification, which unsettles both the powerful and anyone who ranks themselves. The clause about knowing where to place the message says nothing about merit at all, only about the sender's judgement. That closes off two errors at once: resenting who was chosen, and assuming that being chosen indicates anything a person could have arranged for themselves.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the complaint in its plainest form, asking why it did not come to a great man of two cities.
States the principle broadly: your Lord creates and chooses, and the choice is not theirs.
Records a related demand, that each of them be handed scrolls of his own, spread open.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you were passed over and someone else was chosen, and notice whether you concluded anything about your own worth from it. Most of us do. Sit with the possibility that selection tracks something you cannot see, in either direction. That is not consolation. It is a more accurate account of what happened.

studies.title: As If Climbing The Sky
studies.meaning: Two states are described in physical terms. One chest is opened wide for submission, the other made narrow and tight, and then a comparison arrives that has struck readers in every century: as though he were ascending into the sky. Commentators explain it as the breathlessness of climbing beyond where air will support you, which is a remarkably exact description of an experience nobody in that century could have had. What is named is not resistance but constriction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the passage is answering why some accept and some do not after every argument has been made. The surah has offered signs from creation, history, and the shape of revelation itself. This ayah steps behind all of it and describes the receiving state directly, in a Meccan setting where both responses were on display in the same families.
