keyTerms.note: A verb for laying something open, used of cutting meat flat to dry. The same word titles a short surah addressed to the Prophet about his own chest being opened.
Read in two ways by the early authorities, giving either extreme narrowness or a thicket so dense nothing can enter. Both readings survive in the commentaries, and both describe blocked passage.
An intensive form built for difficulty, so the ascent is laboured rather than smooth. The doubling of letters in the Arabic does the work that a whole English phrase about struggling would need.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabs knew altitude from mountains, not from anything higher. Climbing the peaks around Mecca or in the highlands to the south left a person short of breath, and the sensation of the chest working harder for less was familiar to shepherds and to anyone who had walked up out of a valley in the heat. That is the experience the comparison starts from.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for opening the chest here is the same one used at the start of a short late-Meccan surah addressed to the Prophet, asking whether his own chest was not opened for him. The same image therefore describes both what happened to him and what happens to anyone guided.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as a change in capacity rather than in argument, which explains why the surah's long case has convinced some and not others. Something has to be open for anything to enter. The passage attributes both states to God's will while the whole surah holds people responsible, and the mainstream tradition keeps both without collapsing them, treating the constriction as following refusal rather than causing it.

crossReferences.why: Asks about the one whose chest God has opened to submission, so that he stands on a light.
Turns the same image into a prayer, where Moses asks for his own chest to be opened.
Opens a short surah with the same verb, asking whether the chest was not laid open already.

studies.applyIt: Notice where in your body you feel resistance when something true and unwelcome is said to you. For most people it is the chest or the throat, and it arrives before any thought does. Name it once when it happens today. This ayah describes belief and refusal as physical states, and the physical part is the one you can catch.

studies.title: The Home Of Peace
studies.meaning: The path just described is named as the Lord's own, and straight, and the detailed explanation is said to be for people who take a reminder. Then the destination is given a name rather than a description: the Home of Peace, held with their Lord. Commentators note that the word covers safety, wholeness and greeting all at once. The final clause makes God their protector, and attaches that relationship to what they used to do rather than to a status they were granted.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this pair closes the surah's long argument before it turns to specific customs. The audience had been offered warnings for many ayat, and the naming of a destination here is one of the surah's few extended notes of promise. No occasion is reported. The word for peace also functioned as the ordinary Arabian greeting, which gave the name an everyday warmth.

keyTerms.note: The first word means a dwelling with a courtyard, a family compound rather than a house. The second covers safety, soundness and the greeting itself, so the name promises a settled place free of harm.
A form of remembering that means retrieving what is already held. The audience for the detailed explanation is defined by a capacity for recollection rather than by any prior belief.
The relationship the surah has denied to every other candidate, now affirmed. In Arabian usage it named the person who stood behind you, which makes the promise social rather than only spiritual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A home in Arabia meant a walled compound with a courtyard, animals, and several generations inside it. It was where a traveller finally stopped and where safety was assumed rather than negotiated. The greeting of peace was said at its threshold. Naming the destination with that word promised the specific relief of arriving somewhere you no longer have to watch the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The name given here for the final destination appears twice in the Quran, both times in Meccan surahs and both times as a place people are invited to rather than described as inhabiting. The word for peace within it is also one of the names by which God is described elsewhere in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The destination is named by its quality rather than pictured, which is unusual in a book with vivid descriptions available. What is promised first is peace, and only afterwards anything else. The closing clause is careful in a way worth noticing: God is their protector because of what they used to do, so the relationship is tied to a life rather than declared over a category of people.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same name for the destination, saying God invites to the Home of Peace generally.
Gives the greeting spoken at arrival, peace upon you for the patience you kept.
Names the same straight path as a daily request rather than as a description of a group.

studies.applyIt: Say the greeting of peace to one person today whom you would normally pass without speaking: a neighbour, a colleague on another floor, someone at a counter. The word in this ayah names a destination and also names an ordinary courtesy. Using it deliberately once makes the connection between the two audible.

studies.title: We Profited From Each Other
studies.meaning: A gathering is described in which unseen beings are addressed for having taken many humans, and it is their human associates who answer. The answer is unusually candid: we took our enjoyment of one another, and we reached the term You appointed. Commentators note that no defence is offered. The relationship is described as mutual benefit, which is exactly what it was, and the reply that follows names the outcome with an exception attached that the tradition discusses without settling.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the arrangement being described was a working part of Arabian religion. Travellers sought protection from the unseen powers of a place, and men consulted diviners who claimed such contacts, receiving guidance and status in return. Both sides gained something concrete. The ayah does not caricature the relationship; it lets one party describe it accurately.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to seek or acquire a great deal of something. Applied to human beings it treats them as a quantity gathered, which is the ayah's judgement on the relationship stated in a single word.
A verb for deriving use and pleasure from something, the root behind the word for goods and provisions. It names an exchange of advantage, which is how the speakers themselves describe what happened.
From a verb meaning to stay somewhere for a long time. It names a residence rather than a punishment, which makes the sentence a statement of where they now live.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian travellers entering an unfamiliar valley would seek the protection of its resident power before making camp, and diviners in the settlements claimed relationships with such beings that made them consulted and paid. Both arrangements delivered something: a sense of safety on the road, and a livelihood at home. The exchange described in this ayah was a recognised feature of ordinary life.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply in this ayah contains an exception, that they remain except as God wills, and the classical commentators discuss its scope at length without reaching agreement. It is one of the passages where the tradition openly records that the limit of a statement is not settled, and the commentaries preserve the range of readings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a corrupt relationship be described in its own terms and finds that the description condemns it without help. Nobody claims to have been deceived; they say they profited. That places the fault in the exchange itself rather than in a misunderstanding, and it identifies a pattern that survives the specific practice: arrangements in which two parties benefit and something else is spent quietly between them.

crossReferences.why: Shows the other side of the same scene, with the beings themselves disowning those who worshipped them.
Describes the practice as it operated, men seeking refuge in unseen beings and increasing their burden.
Records a similar speech afterwards, in which the tempter admits he had no power beyond an invitation.

studies.applyIt: Think of an arrangement in your life where two people each get something and neither would describe it out loud: a friendship of mutual flattery, a work relationship built on cover. Name what each of you is actually collecting. That is the whole exercise here, and the naming is uncomfortable because it is usually accurate.

studies.title: Wrongdoers Made Allies
studies.meaning: One short ayah states a principle about how alliances form. Some wrongdoers are made close to others, and the reason given is what they used to earn. Commentators read this as describing a natural sorting rather than an imposed punishment: conduct draws like conduct, and people end up among those whose habits match their own. The verb used is the one for making someone a patron or ally, so what is described is not merely company but the protective relationship Arabia was built on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following a scene in which mutual benefit between two parties is admitted openly. The surah has been describing an opposition that acted together, and this ayah explains the mechanism behind such coalitions. No occasion is reported. The observation would have been immediately recognisable in a city where alliances between families shifted according to shared interest.

keyTerms.gloss: We make allies, set as patrons
keyTerms.note: From the root for nearness that gives the word for a protector, used through this surah. It describes assigning one party to another as ally, not merely allowing them to associate.
From a root meaning to put something out of its place. Wrongdoing in Arabic is misplacement, which fits an ayah about people ending up in the company their conduct has sorted them into.
The commercial verb used at the opening of this surah for what God knows of a person. Its return here makes the alliance a return on conduct rather than an accident of circumstance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances were formal and sworn. Two clans would bind themselves to defend each other, and such pacts were remembered for generations and recited in poetry. Choosing an ally was the most consequential decision a family made, and it was made on the basis of shared interest. Everyone understood that you ended up beside people whose way of operating matched your own.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb in this ayah shares its root with the word for a protector that the surah has been using since its early pages, where it asks whether any protector besides God should be taken. The same three letters therefore mark both the relationship that is denied and the one that forms by default.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Company is presented as a consequence rather than a choice made freshly each time. What a person does draws them toward others doing the same, and the passage attributes that sorting to God while tying it explicitly to conduct. The result is a claim worth taking seriously: the circle you find yourself in is information about you, and it accumulated by a process you were participating in without deciding.

crossReferences.why: States the same sorting from both sides, with wrongdoers as allies and God as ally of the mindful.
Describes those who refuse as allies of one another, and warns what follows if that is not answered.
Shows what becomes of such alliances afterwards, when close friends turn into enemies.

studies.applyIt: Look at the five people you spend most time with and ask what habit you all share that none of you would defend. Not the good things, which are easy to see. This ayah says company forms around conduct, which means the shared habit is usually the invisible reason the group works.

studies.title: Messengers From Among You
studies.meaning: The question put at the gathering is procedural. Did messengers not come to you, from among yourselves, relating My signs and warning of this meeting. The phrase from among you is the load-bearing part, since a messenger of one's own kind removes the excuse of not understanding. The answer is a confession rather than a defence, and the ayah adds the explanation without being asked: the life of this world deceived them. Then the confession is repeated, in the narrator's voice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the objection being answered here has run through the surah from its opening pages: that a human messenger was not enough. This ayah puts that objection in the past tense and shows it withdrawn by the people who raised it. The classical commentators discuss the address to both kinds of being, and their readings of how messengers reached the unseen ones vary.

keyTerms.note: Two words that answer the surah's longest-running objection. A messenger of one's own kind is comprehensible and imitable, which is the argument the earlier ayat made about angels at some length.
From the root for following a track, which gives the word for a story. Relating something is described as following its trail, so a narrative is a set of footprints rather than an invention.
The legal verb for giving testimony, used here of the accused testifying against themselves. It turns the scene into a hearing in which the only witness called is the defendant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A proper hearing in Arabia began with establishing that the parties had been informed. A claim could not proceed if a man had never been told of the obligation, and elders would ask first whether notice had been given. The form of the question here follows that procedure exactly, and an audience used to arbitration would have recognised the opening move.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the messengers relating the signs comes from the root that gives the Quran its word for a story, and the same root produces the verb for tracking an animal by its prints. Narrating and tracing a trail are one action in Arabic, which is why a Quranic story is presented as something followed rather than composed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage establishes that nobody is answerable for what they were never told, and it does so by having the parties confirm it themselves. That makes the whole scene procedural rather than vengeful. The explanation slipped in between the two confessions is the ayah's most humane touch. They were deceived by the present life, which is offered not as an excuse but as an accurate account of what actually happened to them.

crossReferences.why: States the principle plainly, that punishment does not come until a messenger has been sent.
Puts the identical question at the gate, and records the same admission that warners did come.
Gives the fullest version of the exchange, including the answer that a warner came and was denied.

studies.applyIt: Think of a warning you have already received more than once about your health, your work, or a relationship. Not a vague worry, an actual warning from someone. Write down what it was in one sentence. This ayah turns on whether notice was given, and most of the notices we are given are forgotten rather than refused.

studies.title: Never While They Were Unaware
studies.meaning: The first ayah gives the reason for the hearing just described. Towns are not destroyed for wrongdoing while their people are unaware, so notice precedes consequence as a matter of principle. Commentators read the unawareness as covering those who never received a message at all. The second ayah then refuses a single verdict for everyone. Each has degrees according to what they did, which means the outcome is graded rather than sorted into two piles, and nothing anyone did has gone unnoticed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a sequence about the questioning at the gathering. The surah has spent many ayat on peoples destroyed before, and this passage supplies the standard those accounts assume. The Meccans, who travelled past ruined settlements twice a year, had been asked repeatedly to consider them. Here they are told what condition every one of those cases satisfied first.

keyTerms.note: From a root for being inattentive to something present. It covers both never having been told and having been told and not attending, and the second ayah's closing clause denies the same quality of God.
Steps of a stair, the same word used earlier in this surah for the raising of Abraham. Its use here for everyone makes the final accounting continuous rather than divided into two categories.
Read by commentators in two ways: destroying them for their wrongdoing, or destroying them unjustly. Both readings are old, and each yields a different emphasis in the same sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian law worked by warning. A tribe intending to act against another gave formal notice, and treaties were publicly renounced before hostilities began, since striking without that step was itself a disgrace. Poetry records the shame of the surprise raid. An audience raised on those conventions would hear this ayah as describing a procedure they already regarded as the mark of honourable dealing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for heedlessness in the first ayah returns at the end of the second, applied to God in the negative. The same term therefore describes the condition that protects people from judgement and the condition that God never occupies, which is a symmetry the Arabic makes visible and translations usually lose.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two principles are stated together and each limits the other. Nobody is held to what they were never given, and everybody is held to what they did, in gradations. The result is a picture of accountability that is neither indiscriminate nor lenient. The final clause also removes the possibility that small acts fall below the threshold of notice, which is where most of a life actually happens.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule for earlier towns, that none was destroyed without warners sent as a reminder.
Applies the principle to a mother city, where a messenger is sent before anything is decided.
Repeats the grading of outcomes by what each person did, so that nobody is treated as a category.

studies.applyIt: Notice a rule you enforce at home or at work that people around you have never actually been told. It might be about tidiness, timing, or tone. Say it out loud once this week before you next hold anyone to it. These ayat make notice the condition of fairness, and the same standard is cheap to apply.

studies.title: Rich Beyond Need, Owner Of Mercy
studies.meaning: Two descriptions are placed side by side, and commentators note that the pairing does the work. God is free of all need, which means nothing is owed to anyone, and He is the owner of mercy, which is why the situation is not what independence alone would produce. What follows is a statement of capacity: He could remove you and put others in your place, exactly as you were raised from the descendants of another people. The second ayah closes with a promise that cannot be evaded.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the reminder about descent from another people had an edge in a city that traced its standing through ancestry. Meccan families held their position by lineage and by inherited offices, and the surah has already argued that guidance does not travel that way. Here even their existence as a people is described as a succession that replaced someone else.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be self-sufficient, which also gives the word for wealth. Applied to God it denies need rather than asserting possession, which is why mercy has to be named separately.
From the root for coming after someone, which gives the word for a successor. It names replacement in an office or a place, so the sentence is about position rather than about destruction.
From a root for weakness and inability, in a form meaning to render someone unable. The denial says nothing anyone does can make the promise fail, which is a claim about capacity, not about effort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia's history was a history of replacement. Tribes displaced tribes at wells and pastures, and the ruins along the trade roads belonged to peoples whose names survived only in poetry. Mecca's own leading tribe had taken custody of the sanctuary from an earlier group within remembered history. Nobody in that audience needed persuading that a people could be succeeded by another.
studies.didYouKnow: The two descriptions opening this passage, free of need and owner of mercy, appear together in this exact pairing only here in the Quran, though each is common on its own. Placed side by side they answer a question the surah has raised repeatedly: why anything at all is given to people who have nothing to offer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Independence and mercy are held together, and neither alone would produce what the passage describes. A God who needed something could be bargained with; a God free of need but without mercy would have no reason to send anything. The reminder about succession then removes any sense of entitlement to a place in the world, while the promise that follows removes the hope of outlasting the account.

crossReferences.why: States the same two ideas: you are the needy ones, and He could remove you and bring a new creation.
Repeats the capacity for replacement plainly, that He could take you away and bring others.
Says the same thing about creation as a whole, and calls it no great matter for God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a role you hold that will one day belong to someone else: a job, a place in a family, a responsibility in a community. Picture the person who will hold it after you, without gloom. Then ask what you would want them to inherit from how you are doing it. That question is usually clarifying within a minute.

studies.title: Work, And So Will I
studies.meaning: The instruction sounds almost like a truce and is not one. Each side is told to work according to its position, and the speaker declares that he is working too. What settles the matter is deferred to knowledge that will arrive rather than to argument now: you will come to know whose is the outcome of the abode. Commentators note the confidence in the closing clause, which states plainly that wrongdoers do not come out ahead, so the deferral is about timing rather than about doubt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this formula appears in several surahs from the same period, always addressed to a community that had run out of arguments to make. It belongs to the stage where persuasion had been attempted at length and was being set down. The classical sources do not record a specific occasion, and the repetition across surahs suggests a standing posture rather than a moment.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place, covering both where a person stands and the standing they have. The word lets the instruction mean work in your own way and according to what you actually are.
From the root for a heel and for following behind, so an outcome is what comes after a thing has passed. The surah has used it earlier when telling listeners to travel and see how peoples ended.
From a root meaning to split open ground for planting, which gives the word for a farmer. Success in Arabic is a harvest reached, so failure here means never arriving at what was worked for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farming in an oasis was a long wager. Ground was cleared, water rights secured and palms planted years before anything came back, and nobody claimed a result until the harvest was in the store. The word for success in this ayah belongs to that world, and it explains why the answer offered here is not an argument but an invitation to wait for the crop.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact instruction, telling opponents to work in their own way while the speaker works in his, appears in three separate places in the Quran, each in a different surah and each spoken by a messenger to his own people. The repetition marks it as the standard closing move when persuasion has been exhausted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models disagreement that has stopped pretending it will be resolved by talking, without becoming hostility. Both sides are told to act, which treats the opponent as a serious agent rather than an obstacle. And the appeal to an outcome rather than to an argument places the matter under time, where it can actually be settled, while the last clause makes clear that the speaker is not neutral about which way it will go.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical instruction in the mouth of an earlier prophet addressing his own community.
Repeats the same formula in another Meccan surah, followed by a promise that they will know.
Describes whose the final home is: those who seek no superiority on earth and cause no corruption.

studies.applyIt: Pick an argument you have been having in your head with someone who is not going to agree, and stop making the case. Instead, spend one hour this week doing the thing you have been trying to justify. This ayah's move is to answer a dispute with work, and it is usually the only answer that lands.

studies.title: This Share Is For God
studies.meaning: A custom is described with unusual precision. Produce and livestock were divided in two, one portion assigned to God and one to the objects of worship beside Him, and then the accounting is exposed. What was set aside for the partners never reached God, while what was set aside for God found its way to them. Commentators explain that shortfalls were made up in one direction only. The closing judgement is brief and is about the arithmetic rather than the theology.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the practice was real and locally documented. Arabian communities allocated a share of harvest and herds for religious purposes, split between the high God and the shrine deities, with the produce used to feed guests, custodians and the poor. The surah's closing section turns from argument to these inherited customs, describing several of them before answering.

keyTerms.note: A verb for scattering and propagating, used of God producing creatures in abundance. Placing it in the sentence reminds the audience whose the crops and herds were before any division was made.
Land that has been ploughed and what grows on it, from the root for tilling. Paired with livestock it covers the two forms of wealth an agricultural society had, so the custom touched everything.
The same phrase used earlier in this surah for assertions made without support. Inserted in the middle of the sentence, it marks the words this is for God as their description rather than the ayah's.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Harvest allocation was public and watched. A family separated portions on the threshing floor while neighbours saw it done, and the shares had names and customary sizes. Livestock were divided in the same way at particular seasons. Because everyone could see the piles, any quiet adjustment between them was a social act as much as a religious one, and people knew who did it.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah preserves an unusually specific piece of pre-Islamic religious practice, describing a division of produce that other sources also record. The Quran's closing section here works almost as a catalogue of such customs, naming four or five distinct ones in a few ayat, and it is one of the earliest documentary sources for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The critique is not that they gave, but that the giving was quietly organised to favour the recipient who could be seen. Everything named was created and provided in the first place, which makes the division a matter of returning rather than donating. That principle reaches past the specific custom. Any portion set aside for God that is later found useful for something else was never really set aside.

crossReferences.why: Records the same practice, assigning a portion of what was provided to what they do not even know.
Asks about provision that people have themselves divided into permitted and forbidden portions.
Addresses the same instinct in giving, not selecting the poorer part to give away.

studies.applyIt: Look at what you set aside for good purposes and check whether any of it quietly comes back to you: a donation that buys standing, help offered where it will be noticed. You do not have to stop. Just find out which portion is actually leaving your hands, since that is what this ayah is measuring.

studies.title: Made To Seem Right
studies.meaning: The gravest of the customs is named, the killing of children, and the ayah is careful about how it happened. It was made to look right to them, so the practice arrived dressed as duty rather than as cruelty. Two purposes are attributed to that dressing: to ruin them, and to confuse their religion until they could no longer tell what belonged to it. Commentators note the sentence about God's will, which denies that the practice was beyond preventing, and the instruction to leave them to their inventions.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the practice was real in parts of Arabia, though the classical sources differ on how widespread it was. Motives recorded include fear of poverty and shame at the birth of daughters. The Quran addresses it in several surahs from this period and always names it directly, without euphemism, which is itself a comment on how it was normally discussed.

keyTerms.note: The same verb the surah uses for conduct dressed up until it looks acceptable. Its appearance here explains how something monstrous was carried out by ordinary people who believed themselves in the right.
From a root meaning to fall into a pit or perish. It names destruction by falling rather than by being struck, which suits a practice adopted step by step and defended each time.
From the root for clothing, so confusion is something laid over a thing. The surah has used the same verb twice already, of confusion put over a question and over a community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Life at the edge of subsistence made every additional dependant a calculation, and drought years forced households into decisions they would not otherwise face. Daughters also carried the risk of capture in a raid, which brought a family lasting shame. These pressures do not excuse anything, and they explain how a custom could be defended by people who thought of themselves as responsible.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this practice in several passages and each time attacks the reasoning rather than only the act, naming the fear of poverty in one place and the shame at a daughter's birth in another. One late Meccan surah puts the question to the child directly, asking for what offence she was killed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies the mechanism by which people do terrible things, which is that the thing is presented to them as right. That is a more useful account than attributing it to wickedness, because it is checkable from the inside. It also names the second damage: once such a practice is folded into religion, the religion itself becomes unreadable, and people lose the ability to tell what it actually asks of them.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the stated motive directly, answering fear of poverty with who provides for whom.
Describes the shame at a daughter's birth and the decision made in secret from the community.
Puts the question to the child herself on that day, asking for what sin she was killed.

studies.applyIt: Notice something your own society finds normal that you suspect will be looked back on with horror. Say what it is, even if only to yourself, and notice how quickly the justifications arrive. That arrival is the mechanism this ayah names, and recognising it working in your own reasoning is the point of the exercise.

studies.title: Reserved For Whom We Please
studies.meaning: Three customs are listed in one ayah. Certain livestock and crops were declared restricted, with access limited to those the owners permitted; certain animals had their backs made off limits so nobody rode them; and over some no name of God was pronounced. Commentators explain each as a vow made about an animal after a number of births or a successful journey. The phrase inserted twice does the work: by their claim, and inventing about Him. The restrictions were real and their attribution was not.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the customs named here are recorded elsewhere in the Quran under their Arabic names and are known from other sources. They were serious commitments. An animal set aside was never worked or sold, which cost the household real wealth, and the practice was regarded as piety. The surah has just described a division of harvest in the same register.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to prevent or enclose, which gives the word for a lap and for a stone enclosure. The term names a barrier put around something rather than a quality the thing has.
The plural of back, naming what was placed off limits. An animal that could not be ridden or loaded was a household's wealth taken permanently out of use, which is what made the vow costly.
The verbal noun from the root used through this surah for fabricating. Placed at the end as a summary, it names the whole set of customs by what they have in common rather than one by one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel dedicated by vow was recognisable and left alone. It grazed where it liked, was not milked for the household, and was never loaded, and everyone in the settlement knew which animal it was. The cost was visible and so was the piety, which is part of why the practice held. Giving up a working animal was a public statement about a family's seriousness.
studies.didYouKnow: A later Medinan passage names four of these dedicated animal categories by their Arabic terms and states that God did not appoint any of them. Between that passage and this one, the Quran preserves a fairly detailed record of pre-Islamic Arabian religious practice that is not documented in this much detail anywhere else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes costly and sincere piety and asks a single question about it, which is where the requirement came from. Sacrifice does not authorise a claim. That is a demanding standard, and it applies as much to restrictions people impose on themselves as to those they impose on others. The phrase about inventing against God places the whole practice in the same category as the surah's gravest charge.

crossReferences.why: Names four of these dedicated animal categories directly and denies that any was appointed by God.
Asks who authorised the division of provision into what is permitted and what is withheld.
Warns against tongues that declare things lawful and unlawful, inventing about God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a personal discipline you keep that costs you something and that you privately regard as a mark of seriousness. Ask where it came from. If it is your own good idea, keep it and call it that. This ayah is not against costly practices; it is against the small upgrade from my practice to God's requirement.

studies.title: Reserved For Our Males
studies.meaning: Another custom is quoted and its structure exposes itself. What is in the wombs of certain animals is reserved for the men and withheld from their wives, and then comes the detail that undoes the whole claim: if it is stillborn, everyone shares. Commentators note the exactness of the observation. A rule presented as a boundary set by God turns out to allocate the valuable portion in one direction and the worthless portion to everyone, which is a distribution rather than a restriction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the surah's closing survey of inherited customs. Arabian food restrictions frequently divided along lines of sex and status, and they were understood as religious obligations rather than as preferences. The Quran's method here is to state each custom in the practitioners' own words and let the arrangement be seen. This one is described with more precision than the others.

keyTerms.note: From the root for something unmixed, which also gives the word for sincerity. Its use for a portion reserved to one group makes the claim of purity sit oddly beside what the rest of the ayah reports.
The plural of a word meaning one of a pair, used for husband and wife alike. Its presence names exactly who was excluded, so the arrangement cannot be described in neutral terms.
A verbal noun for characterising something in a certain way. What will be repaid is named as the describing itself, so the fault is located in the act of labelling rather than only in the practice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat divided at a household was divided by rank, and everyone present could see who received which cut. Women often ate after the men and from what remained. In a subsistence economy these allocations mattered nutritionally, not only symbolically, and a rule reserving the best portion to one group had physical consequences that everyone in the compound experienced.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the exclusive portion in this ayah comes from the root that elsewhere gives the Quran its term for sincerity and for worship made pure for God alone. The same three letters therefore name both undivided devotion and, here, a claim of exclusivity made on a piece of meat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage demonstrates a method rather than only condemning a custom. When a rule claimed to come from God consistently benefits the people who state it, the pattern is itself evidence about where the rule came from. That test does not require any theology to apply, and it is offered to an audience who could check it against their own kitchens. What is repaid, the ayah says, is the description.

crossReferences.why: Applies the same test to another claim, calling a division that favours the claimant an unfair one.
Records the same asymmetry, assigning to God what they did not want for themselves.
Corrects the underlying assumption, since both sons and daughters are given as God wills.

studies.applyIt: Look at a rule in your household or workplace that you helped make, and check who it benefits when it is inconvenient. Not who it was meant to benefit. If the answer is consistently you, that is worth knowing. This ayah's test is simple arithmetic, and it works without anyone needing to be accused of anything.

studies.title: They Forbade What Was Given
studies.meaning: The verdict on the whole sequence arrives, and it puts two very different things in one sentence. Killing children and declaring provision off limits are both named as loss, and both are traced to the same root: acting without knowledge and inventing about God. Commentators note the word used for the folly, which means lightness of mind rather than malice. What is lost is not property but the people themselves, and the closing clause states the outcome twice over.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the survey of inherited customs. The two practices named were not connected in the minds of those who kept them; one was a hard economic decision and the other was piety. The surah joins them because both rested on a claim about what God had established, made by people who had received nothing on the subject. No occasion is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: From a root for lightness and instability, used of a garment flapping loosely. It names a mind without weight rather than a wicked one, which is a specific and less comfortable accusation.

The verb behind the Quranic word for provision, covering food, livelihood and anything that sustains. Its presence makes the restriction a refusal of something already given rather than an act of restraint.
The commercial verb for a deal ending in deficit, used at the opening of this surah of those who lost themselves. The particle before it marks the loss as accomplished rather than threatened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both practices came from the same anxiety about scarcity. A household calculating whether it could feed another mouth and a household setting aside an animal it could not use were both managing an uncertain margin, and both believed they were doing something responsible. The Quran addresses the anxiety directly in other passages by naming who actually provides for whom.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for folly in this ayah is used elsewhere in the Quran of those who are not competent to manage property, and of the one who turns away from the way of Abraham. It describes a lack of weight in judgement, and the classical lexicons connect it to a rope or a garment that will not hold steady.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two practices at opposite ends of severity are traced to one failure, which is speaking for God without having been told anything. That common root is the surah's central concern, and placing an unbearable act beside a merely mistaken one shows how wide the range of consequences from a single error can be. The passage also treats provision as given, so restricting it is described as refusing something rather than as declining it.

crossReferences.why: Asks directly who forbade the good things of provision that God produced for His servants.
Names the fear behind the first practice and answers it with who provides for parent and child alike.
Warns against declaring unlawful the good things made lawful, and against overstepping in either direction.

studies.applyIt: Notice a decision you are making mainly from fear of not having enough: a hesitation about hospitality, an unwillingness to commit time. Name the fear rather than the reason you usually give. This ayah traces two very different failures to the same anxiety, and the anxiety is easier to address than the decisions built on it.

studies.title: Give Its Due At Harvest
studies.meaning: After the false restrictions comes the real instruction, and it has three parts. Eat of the fruit when it yields, give its due on the day of harvest, and do not be excessive. Commentators differ over what exactly the due refers to, some reading it as the later obligatory portion and others as the general giving to the poor at harvest time, and the tradition records the range. The timing is the striking detail: on the day, before the crop has become a stored possession.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this places the instruction before the detailed Medinan arrangements for giving were established, which is why the commentators differ about its scope. The gardens described, some trellised and some not, belong to the oasis agriculture of the region rather than to Mecca's own barren valley. The passage answers the preceding customs by describing what was actually asked.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a structure raised up, used of vines trained over frames. Pairing it with untrellised covers cultivated and wild growth, so nothing that grows falls outside the sentence.
The word for a right owed rather than a favour offered. Calling the portion a due makes the recipient a claimant, which changes the posture of both giver and receiver.
From a root for going past a proper limit. Commentators apply it to both consumption and giving, since exceeding what is reasonable in generosity was also understood as a form of excess.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Harvest day was public in an oasis. The dates were cut, piled and divided while neighbours and the poor of the settlement were present, and the customary shares were handed out on the spot rather than sent later. Giving at that moment cost nothing extra in effort and was visible to everyone. Once the crop went into store, it belonged to the household in a different way.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about not being excessive appears in an almost identical form in another Meccan surah, attached there to eating and drinking. Both times it closes with the same clause about what God does not love, and the pairing of a permission with a limit in one sentence is characteristic of these passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction begins with permission and ends with a limit, and the giving sits between them, which is a structure worth noticing. Enjoyment is not treated as suspect. What is asked is that a portion is recognised as owed at the moment the wealth arrives, before ownership has settled. Calling that portion a due rather than a gift removes the giver's advantage over the recipient entirely.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle about wealth generally, that a known share belongs to those in need.
Repeats the closing clause about excess almost word for word, applied to eating and drinking.
Extends the warning about waste, calling the wasteful brothers of the devils.

studies.applyIt: The next time money arrives unexpectedly, give a portion of it away on the same day rather than when you have thought about it. The timing is the whole instruction here. A sum that has sat in your account for a week feels like yours in a way that a sum arriving this morning does not.

studies.title: The Footsteps Of An Enemy
studies.meaning: Livestock are described by their uses, some large enough to carry loads and some kept low for other benefits, and commentators differ over the exact sense of the second word. Then two instructions follow. Eat of what God provided, which reopens what the customs had closed, and do not follow the footsteps of the enemy. The image is precise: not his commands but his footprints, meaning a path walked one step at a time by someone who never decided to take it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the passage is dismantling a system of inherited restrictions that had accumulated gradually. Nobody in the city had adopted the whole set at once; each generation had received it and added to it. The image of following footsteps rather than orders describes exactly that process, which is why it appears here rather than in a passage about open defiance.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for carrying, naming animals large enough to bear loads. It classifies livestock by function rather than by kind, which is how a herding household actually thought about them.
From the root for spreading something out, and read by commentators as smaller animals close to the ground, or as what their wool and hides are spread out to make. Both senses are preserved.
The plural of a single stride. Following footprints is different from obeying instructions, since each step is small, plausible and connected only to the one before it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tracking was a universal skill. A herdsman could read from prints in sand which animal had passed, how long ago, and whether it was loaded, and children learned to follow a trail before they could read anything else. Following footsteps was therefore an image of something done confidently and half-consciously, eyes on the ground, without needing to know where the trail leads.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about following the footsteps of the enemy appears four times in the Quran, and every occurrence is in a passage about ordinary conduct rather than about grand wrongdoing: food, wealth, gossip and the treatment of others. The image is reserved for gradual drift rather than for dramatic rebellion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is described as forming through steps rather than decisions, which is both a warning and a relief. Nobody chooses a whole direction at once, so nobody has to reverse one at once either. The instruction to eat what was provided also matters here. Undoing an unwarranted restriction is treated as part of good conduct, not as laxity, which keeps the passage from being read as a call for more caution.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase, joining permission to eat what is good with the warning about footsteps.
Applies the same image to speech and reputation, where the first step looks entirely harmless.
Describes livestock by their benefits at greater length, including warmth, food and transport.

studies.applyIt: Think of a habit you would not have accepted three years ago and trace the individual steps that got you there. There will be about five, and each will have been reasonable. This ayah's image is a trail rather than a decision, and trails can be walked back the same way they were walked in.

studies.title: Eight Pairs Of Livestock
studies.meaning: The argument becomes forensic. Eight pairs are counted out, beginning with sheep and goats, and then the question is put with no room left in it: was it the two males that were withheld, or the two females, or what the females carry. Every possibility is enumerated, so no answer can be improvised. Commentators note that the customs being challenged did not fall neatly into any of these categories, which is the point. The demand that closes it is for knowledge, not for an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the counting is deliberate. The audience's restrictions applied to particular animals in particular circumstances, arrived at by vows and inherited practice rather than by any principle. Setting the whole herd out as eight pairs and asking which category was named forces a general rule to be produced where only particular customs existed.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for one of a pair, so eight pairs means four kinds counted by male and female. The Quran uses the same word of human spouses and of created things generally.
From the root for a garment wrapped around the body. Applied to a womb it describes enclosure rather than possession, which keeps the third option in the question distinct from the first two.
An imperative from the root behind the words for weighty news and for a prophet. Demanding information in that form asks for something with a source behind it, not for a report of what people do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The four animals named were the whole of a household's wealth. Sheep and goats gave milk, wool and meat and were counted daily; camels carried loads and crossed deserts; cattle worked the land at the oases. A man's standing was stated in numbers of these, and dividing them into eight pairs was how anyone would have taken an inventory.
studies.didYouKnow: The counting of livestock as eight pairs appears again in another surah, where it is listed among God's provisions rather than used as an argument. The same enumeration therefore serves twice, once as a description of what was given and once as the frame for a question about what was withheld.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage insists that a claim about God's requirements be stated as a general rule that can be examined, and the demand for knowledge at the end sets the standard. This is a method rather than a doctrine, and it applies wherever practice hardens into obligation. Listing creation as pairs also does quiet work, since the animals under dispute are presented first as things given before they are argued about.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same eight pairs among what was sent down for people, without any argument attached.
Names pairing as a feature of creation generally, among humans and among the livestock alike.
Describes what these animals were given for, which the customs under dispute had partly cancelled.

studies.applyIt: Take a rule you have been told is required and try to state it as a general principle, in one sentence, without naming the particular case. Some rules survive this and some do not. The ayah's method is exactly that translation, and it usually takes about a minute to find out which kind you have.

studies.title: Were You There To Witness
studies.meaning: The same enumeration is repeated for camels and cattle, and then a new question is added that goes past the content to the source. Were you present when God charged you with this. Commentators note that the demand shifts from producing a rule to producing an occasion, which nobody could do. The ayah then names the wrongdoing directly and adds a purpose clause absent earlier: inventing about God in order to mislead people, which makes the fault social as well as personal.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, completing the challenge begun in the previous ayah. Religious authority in Arabia rested on inherited custom, and nobody claimed a moment of instruction behind it. The question about being present therefore had no available answer, which the surah knows. It is asked to make the absence of any source audible rather than to receive a reply.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both being present at an event and testifying to it. The question uses the first sense to expose the absence of the second, since no one can testify to what they did not attend.
A verb for entrusting an instruction to someone, used for a solemn charge and for a will. The same verb returns a few ayat later, introducing what God actually did enjoin.
A purpose clause naming the effect of the invention on other people. It turns a private fabrication into an act with victims, which is why the ayah's judgement is stated in its strongest form.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony in Arabia meant having been there. A man's word carried weight in proportion to whether he had witnessed the event himself, and hearsay was recognised as weaker even where nothing was written down. Asking whether someone was present when an instruction was given was a standard move in a dispute, and everyone knew what an evasive answer to it meant.
studies.didYouKnow: The question about being present when something was decreed appears in a similar form in another surah, asked there of people who described the angels as female. Both times the challenge is the same: a claim about the unseen is met not with a counterargument but with a question about attendance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a standard for religious claims that is procedural rather than doctrinal, asking where a rule came from before asking whether it is right. That standard is uncomfortable in every generation, since much of what any community treats as required arrived without an occasion anyone can name. The added clause about misleading others makes clear why the Quran treats this as the gravest category of wrong.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question of another claim, whether they witnessed the creation of what they describe.
States the same judgement earlier in this surah, on inventing against God or denying His signs.
Names the practice directly, tongues declaring things permitted or withheld and inventing about God.

studies.applyIt: Ask about one religious practice you keep whether you could say where it comes from, in one sentence, to someone who asked sincerely. If you cannot, that is a research task rather than a reason to stop. This ayah's question is about sources, and knowing yours makes a practice steadier rather than shakier.

studies.title: Nothing That I Find
studies.meaning: The answer to a long argument is a report rather than a ruling. He does not find, in what was revealed to him, anything withheld from someone eating except a short and specific list. Commentators note the wording, which describes searching a text and reporting the result, so nothing is being decided in the moment. What closes the ayah is not a warning. Someone driven to it by necessity, without seeking it out or overstepping, is met with two names of mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and this is the surah's direct answer to the customs it has been describing. The list given is short, and other passages in the Quran give it in nearly identical terms. The commentators discuss its relation to those parallels at length. What is agreed is the contrast being drawn: an elaborate inherited system on one side, and a brief answer on the other.

keyTerms.note: The verb for finding something on searching. Reporting a search rather than issuing a decision keeps the speaker in the position of a reader of what was given, which the whole surah has insisted on.
From a root for raising the voice, which also gives the word for a new crescent moon greeted with shouts. It names the act of announcing a name aloud, which is what makes the dedication meaningful.
Two names that close many Quranic passages where a limit has just been stated. The first covers what is concealed and pardoned, the second a mercy that is given rather than earned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Necessity was not hypothetical. Famine years, a caravan that ran short, or a family cut off by drought put people in front of decisions they would never otherwise face, and the sources describe communities in real starvation. The clause about compulsion was not written for an unusual case. It answered a situation many in the audience had seen or would see.
studies.didYouKnow: This list appears in four places across the Quran, in Meccan and Medinan surahs, and every occurrence carries the same clause about someone compelled by necessity. The consistency is unusual for a passage of this kind, and the commentators treat the repeated exception as inseparable from the list itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Brevity is the argument. After many ayat describing customs added by inheritance and vow, the answer is short enough to remember, which says something about the difference between what was given and what accumulated around it. The closing names then govern the whole passage. A limit that ends in forgiveness and mercy is a different kind of thing from one that ends in a threat, and the ayah puts them in that order.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same short list with the same exception, in another Meccan setting.
Repeats the list and the clause about compulsion, adding that God is forgiving and merciful.
Sets out the fullest version in a Medinan surah, ending again with the exception for necessity.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know who is in a hard situation and has done something you would not do. Before judging it, ask what their options actually were. This ayah attaches an exception for necessity to every statement of a limit, and applying the same courtesy to a person you know takes only a moment's imagination.

studies.title: That Was Their Recompense
studies.meaning: A different and longer set of restrictions is described, given to an earlier community, and the ayah is specific about which parts were included and which were not. Commentators note the detail, since the exceptions are named as carefully as the restrictions. The reason given is stated plainly: this was a recompense for a particular transgression, so the limits were consequences rather than permanent features. The ayah then closes with an assertion of truthfulness about the account itself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the comparison is being made for the audience in front of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The surah has just described customs invented without authority; here it describes limits that had a source and a stated reason. Other passages in the Quran describe the same restrictions in similar terms, and the classical commentaries read the two accounts together.

keyTerms.note: The word for a claw or an undivided hoof, and the commentators differ over how widely it extends. The range of their readings is preserved rather than settled, which is characteristic of the vocabulary here.
The plural of a word for animal fat, a valuable food in a lean economy. Naming the exceptions in detail keeps the restriction bounded rather than sweeping, which is the ayah's evident concern.
From a root for seeking and then for exceeding a limit. It names a specific transgression rather than a character, which is why the ayah gives a reason instead of a verdict on a people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities following earlier scriptures lived across the region and in Arabian towns, trading and farming alongside their neighbours, and their food practices were visible and known. Meccans travelling north encountered them regularly. The audience for this ayah therefore had a working familiarity with the restrictions being described, which is why they could be named without explanation.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes these restrictions in two other places, and one of them adds a detail worth noting: that all food had been permitted before, apart from what one forefather had withheld from himself. The three passages together present the limits as arising within history rather than as belonging to it from the start.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a distinction the surrounding ayat depend on. Restrictions can come from God, in which case they have a source, a scope and a reason, or they can accumulate without any of the three. Naming a cause for these limits keeps them intelligible rather than arbitrary, and the closing statement about truthfulness attaches to the account, which the surah is offering as something checkable rather than asserted.

crossReferences.why: Notes that food had been permitted before, apart from what one forefather withheld from himself.
Describes the same limits and gives the same reason, naming the specific conduct behind them.
Refers back to this passage and adds that the wrong done was to themselves rather than to God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a restriction you live under that arrived as a consequence of something: a rule at work after an incident, a limit in a relationship after a breach. Ask whether the reason still holds. Rules with reasons can be revisited, and this ayah is careful to give one, which is what makes that possible.

studies.title: Mercy Wide, Yet Not Averted
studies.meaning: The instruction for being called a liar is not a defence. Tell them their Lord possesses a mercy that is wide, and then add the second half without softening either. Commentators note the order, since mercy is named first and at greater length, and the word used for its breadth is the one applied elsewhere to knowledge that takes everything in. The second clause states a limit that is not about severity but about direction: what comes is not turned back from those who have earned it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the accusation of lying was constant rather than occasional. The surah has recorded it in several forms already. Placing a statement about mercy in the mouth of someone who has just been called a liar is a striking choice, and the classical sources treat it as characteristic of the Meccan period, when the answer to hostility was repeatedly a description of God rather than a rebuttal.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for containing something with room to spare, used earlier in this surah of God's knowledge. Applied to mercy it says the same thing: nothing falls outside for lack of capacity.
A passive verb for something sent back the way it came. The denial is about deflection rather than about force, so what is described is a consequence that cannot be redirected once it is moving.
From a root for cutting or severing, connected to harvesting. The word names people by their acts rather than by their beliefs, which keeps the category defined by conduct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A protector in Arabia could shelter a man from consequences, and the whole system of clan patronage worked by turning claims aside. A powerful patron could make a debt or a blood claim simply stop. Everyone in the audience knew that the question was never whether you were guilty but whether someone would stand between you and the claim. This ayah addresses that expectation directly.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of an assurance of mercy with a statement of consequence occurs repeatedly in the Quran, often within a single ayah, and the mercy is almost always named first. The classical commentaries treat the ordering as deliberate, so that hope is established before any limit is described.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both halves are given to the same audience at the same moment, which resists the instinct to sort people into those who need encouragement and those who need warning. The passage assumes a listener can hold both. The word used for mercy's breadth also matters: it is not that mercy is large enough for most cases, but that capacity is not the constraint at all, which places the question entirely elsewhere.

crossReferences.why: States the same breadth directly, that His mercy encompasses everything there is.
Puts the assurance in its most open form, addressed to those who have gone furthest against themselves.
Places forgiveness, acceptance of repentance and severity in one sequence of names.

studies.applyIt: Notice which half of this you usually reach for, whether you tend to comfort people or to warn them. Most of us lean one way and think it is balance. Once this week, say the half you would normally leave out, in the same conversation. The ayah gives both to the same listener in one sentence.

studies.title: Had God Willed, We Would Not
studies.meaning: The objection is predicted before it is made, and it is the strongest one available to them. If God had willed otherwise, none of this would have happened, so the practice is evidence of His will. Commentators note that the ayah does not deny the premise. It observes that earlier peoples argued the same way and that the argument did not protect them, and then it asks for what the objection lacks: any knowledge that could be produced. What is left is conjecture and estimation.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the argument recorded here was in active use. The surah has already stated more than once that God could have gathered everyone onto guidance, so the objectors were quoting a principle the message itself affirmed. The classical commentators treat the response as addressing the use being made of a true statement rather than the statement itself.

keyTerms.note: The verb of tasting used through this surah for consequence experienced directly. Its appearance here marks the end of the earlier peoples' argument, which was not refuted but simply overtaken by events.

keyTerms.gloss: so you may bring it out
keyTerms.note: A verb for producing something from where it is kept, as goods are brought out for inspection. The demand is for evidence to be shown rather than described, which is what an appeal to knowledge means here.
The technical term for assessing a standing crop by eye, used earlier in this surah of the majority. Its return here labels a theological argument with a word from agricultural approximation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fate was a serious idea in pre-Islamic Arabia. Poetry attributes deaths, losses and fortunes to time or to fate, and the attitude ran deep enough to shape how people spoke about their own choices. The objection recorded here was not invented for the occasion. It drew on an existing habit of explaining what had happened by saying it was always going to.
studies.didYouKnow: This objection is quoted in at least three places in the Quran, in almost identical words each time, and it is never answered by denying that God's will governs events. The response is always about what the speakers can actually produce, which is a consistent handling of the same argument across separate surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes between a truth and the use made of it. That God's will governs what happens is affirmed throughout the Quran, including a few ayat later. What the objectors do is convert it into a defence, and the answer points out that they have no access to the premise they are invoking. Nobody can consult God's will in advance, so it cannot function as a reason for a course of action already chosen.

crossReferences.why: Records the same objection almost word for word, and answers by describing what messengers were for.
Preserves another version of it, adding that they have no knowledge of what they assert.
Follows immediately and affirms the premise itself, that He could have guided everyone.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself explaining a choice you made by saying it was meant to be, or that you had no option. Sometimes that is true. Once today, when you hear yourself say it, ask what you would have done differently if you had believed the choice was yours. The answer is usually available immediately.

studies.title: The Conclusive Argument
studies.meaning: Two short clauses, and the second concedes what the objectors had just claimed. The conclusive argument belongs to God, and had He willed, He would have guided everyone. Commentators note the word for the argument, which names the case that reaches its destination and settles a dispute. What is denied is not the premise but its ownership. The objectors were using God's will as their argument; the ayah says the argument that arrives is His, and then affirms exactly what they said.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed immediately after the objection it answers. The surah has been making a sustained case for many ayat, and this is close to its final word on the matter of who can settle it. No occasion is reported. The pairing of the two ayat, objection and answer, is one of the clearest examples of the surah's method of quoting an argument fully before responding.

keyTerms.note: The decisive case in a dispute, the same word used earlier in this surah of the reasoning given to Abraham. Both times it is described as belonging to God rather than to the person making it.
From the verb for arriving at a destination, used earlier in this surah of the recitation reaching whomever it reaches. An argument described this way is one that gets all the way there.
An emphatic word for totality placed at the end for weight. It closes off any reading in which some would have been guided and others left, which is the softening a listener might have looked for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dispute in Arabia ended when one side produced a case the other could not answer, and everyone present recognised the moment. The word for such an argument was in ordinary use. Saying that the conclusive one belongs to God described the end of a hearing rather than a stage in it, and an audience trained on public arbitration would have heard exactly that.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a conclusive argument appears in the Quran a handful of times, and once in a passage explaining why messengers were sent at all: so that people would have no argument against God afterwards. The same term therefore marks both what God holds and what human beings are left without.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah affirms an uncomfortable premise rather than dodging it, and the affirmation is what makes the preceding answer honest. God could have guided everyone and did not. What the passage refuses is the move from that fact to a defence, since nobody can invoke a decision they were not party to. The result is a position that concedes everything about divine will and concedes nothing about human responsibility.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word, saying messengers were sent so that no argument would remain against God.
States the same conditional about people being made one community, and what followed instead.
Holds both sides in two lines: whoever wills may take a way, and willing itself is within God's will.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between accepting that something was in God's hands after it happens and using that to decide what to do beforehand. The first is trust and the second is not. Pick one decision you are facing and make it on the reasons available to you, then hand the outcome over afterwards. That order is what this ayah preserves.

studies.title: Bring Your Witnesses Forward
studies.meaning: The challenge becomes a summons. Bring your witnesses who will testify that God withheld this, and then an instruction follows that anticipates their appearing: if they testify, do not testify with them. Commentators note the assumption built into the sentence, that witnesses could well be produced and that their number would prove nothing. The rest of the ayah names three things about the people whose inclinations are not to be followed, and each is a description rather than an insult.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the summons uses the vocabulary of Arabian dispute settlement, where a claim was supported by producing men who would swear to it. Numbers and standing mattered more than what the witnesses had actually seen. The surah has been asking for a source for these customs across several ayat, and this is the last and most formal version of the request.

keyTerms.note: An imperative of summoning, unchanged for number or gender in the dialect the Quran preserves. Its abruptness gives the challenge the tone of a courtroom rather than of a discussion.
A prohibition against joining a testimony, not against hearing it. It separates the act of witnessing from the act of being present, which is the distinction on which the whole instruction rests.
The same verb that closes the very first ayah of this surah, where those who refuse set up equals to their Lord. Its return here brings the surah's argument back to where it began.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Producing witnesses was how a case was won. A man with more supporters of higher standing prevailed, and the content of what they swore to was often less important than who they were. Testimony was an act of alignment as much as of reporting. That is precisely why the instruction here separates being present from adding your own voice to what is said.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that closes this ayah is the same one that closes the opening ayah of the surah, which describes those who set up equals to their Lord. More than a hundred and forty ayat apart, the two occurrences frame the whole argument, so the surah's closing challenge returns to the word it began with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truthfulness is treated as something separate from consensus, and the instruction makes the separation practical. Others may testify, and you are not required to contradict them, only not to join. That is a workable form of integrity for someone outnumbered, which is what the audience for this ayah was. The passage also connects following inclinations to disbelief in the hereafter, since what a person can afford to affirm depends on what they expect.

crossReferences.why: Describes standing firm as witnesses for God even against oneself or one's own relatives.
Asks who does greater wrong than one who conceals a testimony that he holds from God.
Asks the same question a few ayat earlier, whether they were present when this was enjoined.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time a group agreed on something you did not believe and you nodded along. The ayah does not ask you to argue. It asks you not to add your own voice to it, which is a smaller and much more achievable thing. Practise the silence once, and notice how little it costs.

studies.title: Come, I Will Recite It
studies.meaning: A public invitation opens the list. The phrasing is careful. What follows is what your Lord has forbidden, recited rather than argued. The items are mostly prohibitions, with one positive command about parents. That command sits inside the series rather than beside it. Killing children out of poverty is answered mid-sentence with a statement about provision. Early scholars note that indecency is named in both its open and its hidden forms.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the end of a surah that has spent its length disputing with people over what they had declared off limits on their own authority. The verses just before challenge those self-made bans. This passage answers by reciting what was actually laid down. Early scholars treat the sequence as deliberate. A false list is set aside and a true one is read out in its place.

keyTerms.note: An imperative meaning to come towards a higher place, used to call someone over. It opens the passage as an invitation rather than a summons, and it is addressed to opponents in the middle of a dispute.
Not general hardship but the condition of having nothing left at all. The word names the actual pressure behind the practice being addressed, which the verse answers by naming who provides.
The plural of a word for what is excessive and shameful. The verse divides it into what appears and what is hidden, so the category is defined by the act rather than by whether anyone saw it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burying an infant in a famine is attested in the poetry and the reports of Arabia before Islam. It was driven by the sums of a bad season. In a household with no reserve, there were mouths that could not be fed. The Quran addresses the practice more than once. Each time it attaches a statement about provision to the ban. That answers the calculation, not only the act.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage and the two verses after it have been read since early times as a parallel to the commandments given to Moses. Classical scholars note the resemblance directly. The list here begins where those do, with associating nothing with God and honouring parents. It closes with a call to understand rather than with a threat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list is introduced as recitation. That puts its authority outside the speaker. That is the whole point of the surah's argument. There is a difference between what God has laid down and what a community has decided among itself. Placing kindness to parents inside a series of bans has been read a certain way. It shows that some duties cannot be met by holding back alone. The stated purpose at the end is understanding.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the prohibition on killing children from fear of poverty, reversing the order of provision.
Continues the same recitation through weights, speech, and the straight path.
Lists what has actually been forbidden, open indecency and hidden alike.

studies.applyIt: The verse divides wrongdoing into what shows and what does not. Pick the quietest item on your own list, the thing nobody would ever hear about, and do one concrete thing this week that makes continuing it harder. Not a resolution, an arrangement. The hidden half is the half that survives on being unmentioned.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to read out what God has really forbidden. The list says not to set anything beside God, to be good to your parents, and not to kill your children out of poverty. God feeds you all.

studies.title: Even If It Concerns A Relative
studies.meaning: Four things are set out together and the arrangement is deliberate. Property held for a child who cannot yet defend it, weights and measures at the market, speech given about someone, and the covenant with God. Commentators note the clause inserted in the middle, that no soul is charged beyond its capacity, which softens the standard for measuring without lowering it. The hardest item is the third, since fairness in speech is required even where a close relative is involved.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and part of a short sequence that reads like a summary of what was actually enjoined, set against the customs the surah has just dismantled.
