Orphans were numerous in a society where men died young in raids and on journeys, and their property passed into the keeping of relatives with no external oversight. Measures at the seasonal fairs were similarly unpoliced.

keyTerms.note: From the root for firmness and strength, naming the age at which a person can manage their own affairs. Commentators differ over the exact point, and the tradition records a range of readings.
A word for a share correctly apportioned, distinct from the general term for justice. Its root sense is dividing something into due portions, which suits an instruction about weights and measures.
From the root for balance and equality, the same one used at the surah's opening for setting up equals to God. Applied to speech it asks for an account that does not lean.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Weights and measures were personal property. A merchant carried his own stones and his own measuring vessel, and a small variation between the set used for buying and the set used for selling was invisible and profitable. Orphans' estates were held on the same trust basis, with no register anywhere. Both arrangements ran entirely on the character of the person holding them.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about no soul being burdened beyond its capacity appears three times in the Quran, and here it sits in the middle of an instruction about measuring. Its placement is unusual, and the classical commentators read it as acknowledging that perfect exactness in a weighing is not achievable, while intention is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Each item names a situation where nobody would find out. A child cannot audit an estate, a customer cannot check a stone, and an account given about a relative is not verified against anything. Placing the covenant with God at the end of that list is the passage's argument: what holds in unwitnessed situations is a relationship rather than a rule, which is why the four belong in one sentence.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair almost word for word, orphan property and full measure with a straight balance.
Describes the exact fraud named here, taking full measure from others and giving less in return.
Extends fairness in testimony to cases against oneself, parents and near relatives alike.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you described a disagreement involving someone close to you. Tell it again, to yourself, with the other side's version given the same room. That is the third item on this list and the one most of us fail without noticing, because nobody is ever there to check the account.

studies.title: One Path And Many Ways
studies.meaning: A contrast is drawn in the grammar itself. The path is singular and described as straight; the alternatives are plural and unnamed. Following them is said to scatter you from His way, and commentators note the verb, which describes a group being pulled apart rather than an individual losing direction. Nothing is said about where the other ways lead. What is named is only the effect of taking them, which is fragmentation, and the purpose given at the end is mindfulness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the short sequence of what was actually enjoined. The surah has spent its final section describing customs that accumulated in different directions, so a warning about many ways answers something concrete rather than abstract. The classical commentators record a report in which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) drew a single line and lines branching from it to illustrate this ayah.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a track or route, set against the singular term used for the path. Arabic marks the contrast by number alone, which the translation has to do with an adjective.
An intensive verb for a group breaking into separate pieces. The object is the people rather than the road, so what the other routes do first is divide those walking, not mislead them.
The same verb that closes the two ayat before this one, marking the end of each instruction. Its repetition binds the short sequence together as a single charge rather than three separate ones.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan held together by staying on one route. Where tracks branched, a party that split at a fork could lose contact for days or permanently, since there was no way to signal across distance. Guides argued about routes and the arguments mattered. Everyone travelling in that country understood that the danger of a fork was separation before it was ever the wrong destination.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical collections preserve a report describing the Prophet drawing a straight line in the sand and then short lines branching off it, saying that the first was the way and pointing at the others as paths with something calling from each. The image is remembered chiefly because it explains this ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Unity is presented as an effect of direction rather than as a separate obligation, which is a distinctive claim. People are not asked to hold together and also to follow the path; following the path is what keeps them together, and leaving it is described first by what it does to the group. The purpose stated at the end is mindfulness rather than correctness, which keeps the instruction from becoming a matter of position alone.

crossReferences.why: Names the same single way given across the prophets, and warns against becoming divided in it.
Uses the same structure: a way ordained to be followed, against the inclinations of those without knowledge.
Turns the same straight path into the request recited in every unit of the daily prayer.

studies.applyIt: Notice a disagreement in your community that is about method rather than about anything essential. Ask what it would take for the two sides to keep walking together while still disagreeing. This ayah's first warning is about scattering, which means the cost of a branch is usually paid in company before it is paid in direction.

studies.title: Complete For The One Who Did Well
studies.meaning: Four things are said about the Book given to Moses, and the first is the least expected: it was a completion for the one who did well. Commentators read this in more than one way, either as completing what such a person had already been given or as a favour completed upon them, and the tradition holds both. The other three are detail, guidance and mercy. The purpose stated at the end is belief in meeting their Lord, which is the same thing this surah has been arguing for throughout.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the mention of Moses at this point serves the surah's argument. The audience acknowledged that an earlier Book existed and was known in the region, and the passage that follows uses that acknowledgement to remove an excuse. The classical sources do not attach this ayah to an occasion, and the Arabic word that opens it has been read by commentators as marking sequence in narration rather than in time.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun for bringing something to its full state. Read either as completing a favour or as completing what was already held, and the classical commentaries record both without deciding.
From the root for beauty and excellence, so the verb means doing something well rather than merely doing it. The same root gave this surah its word for the prophets in the earlier list.

keyTerms.gloss: and a setting out in detail
keyTerms.note: The noun from the verb used repeatedly in this surah for separating something into its parts. Applied to a scripture it describes a text laid out so that its pieces can be distinguished.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities holding the earlier scripture lived along the trade roads north and in the towns of Arabia, and Meccan merchants dealt with them regularly. That a Book had been given to Moses was common knowledge in the region rather than a claim requiring support. It is precisely because the fact was uncontroversial that the argument built on it in the following ayat works.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one after it use nearly the same vocabulary for two different scriptures, describing each as sent down and each as carrying guidance and mercy. Placing the two descriptions in consecutive ayat is the surah's way of stating continuity without arguing for it explicitly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as completing something rather than replacing it, and the completion is directed at a person who was already doing well. That order matters: the Book meets existing goodness and finishes it rather than creating it from nothing. And the stated purpose, belief in meeting their Lord, ties an entire scripture to the single conviction the surah has been defending since its opening pages.

crossReferences.why: Names the same giving, the Scripture and the criterion, so that they might be guided.
Refers to the same Book and makes it a reason not to doubt the meeting being described.
Describes it as guidance and a reminder inherited by those who came after him.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good practice you already have that could be finished rather than replaced: a habit of generosity without regularity, a reading habit without direction. This ayah describes a completion given to someone already doing well. Add the missing piece to one such practice this week rather than starting something new.

studies.title: Lest You Should Say
studies.meaning: A purpose is given for this Book that is stated negatively, and it is unusual. It came so that a particular sentence could no longer be spoken: that scripture was given to two communities before us and we knew nothing of what they studied. Commentators identify the two communities as those holding the earlier scriptures. The excuse being removed is not disbelief but distance, the reasonable complaint of people who had heard that revelation existed elsewhere and had never received any in their own language.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the complaint was genuine. Arabs knew that scriptural communities existed nearby, and they knew those scriptures were studied in languages they did not read. Some in the region had begun searching for something equivalent before the message came. The passage addresses a real grievance rather than a hypothetical one, which is why it is answered by removal rather than by rebuke.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to kneel and settle, giving the idea of good that comes to rest in a place. The same description was applied to this Book earlier in the surah, in a passage about warning a city.
A dual form for two distinct parties, from a root meaning to go around something. The dual is precise: the complaint named two known communities rather than scripture-holders in general.
From the root for reading a text repeatedly until it is learned, the same verb used earlier in this surah in the accusation that he had studied. The word names sustained schooling in a text.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture was studied aloud in languages Arabs did not know. A Meccan trader in a northern town would see a community gathered around a reader working through a text he could not follow, and would understand that something of weight was being handled there and was not available to him. That experience, repeated over generations, is the exact complaint these ayat quote.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for study comes from the same root as the verb in the accusation, a few pages earlier, that the Prophet had been taught by someone. The same term therefore appears twice in this surah, once as a charge against him and once in the excuse that his people would have made without him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as closing an excuse, which places the whole subject inside fairness rather than favour. Nobody is to be answerable for what was only ever available in a language and a community not their own. That is a claim about how God deals with people generally, and it implies something further: wherever a genuine excuse of ignorance exists, it is treated as genuine.

crossReferences.why: Describes this same Book in nearly identical words earlier in the surah, with a different purpose attached.
Names the earlier scriptures given before, which the two communities in this complaint held.
Voices the same excuse from the other end, asking why no messenger was sent before the consequence.

studies.applyIt: Notice an excuse you use that is actually true: not enough time, never taught, nobody showed you. Some of them are fair. Pick one and ask what would have to change for it to stop being available. These ayat treat a real excuse seriously and then remove it, which is a different thing from dismissing it.

studies.title: We Would Have Been Better Guided
studies.meaning: The second excuse is confidence rather than ignorance: had a Book come to us, we would have made better use of it than they did. Commentators note the tone, which assumes that the earlier communities failed through some deficiency the speakers do not share. The answer arrives without argument. Clarification has now come, and guidance, and mercy, so the claim can be tested rather than asserted. The rest of the ayah names what turning away from it amounts to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the sentiment is recorded elsewhere in the Quran as an oath sworn before the message came, that if a warner reached them they would be more guided than any nation. The surah quotes the claim after the message has arrived, which changes its status entirely. It is no longer a boast about a possibility but a description of what did not happen.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root for finding a way. Comparing one's own hypothetical performance to another community's actual record is the exact form the ayah is quoting, and the comparative carries it.

Something that makes a matter plain, the same word used earlier in this surah when the speaker says he stands on clear evidence from his Lord. Its return here places the same thing in the listeners' hands.

A less common verb for veering away, used earlier in this surah of people shying from the signs. It is repeated three times in this one ayah, which is unusual and makes turning away the sentence's subject.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs took considerable pride in their memory and their language, and regarded the retention of poetry and genealogy as evidence of a superior faculty. A community that could hold thousands of lines of verse without writing had reason to think it would handle a text well. The boast quoted here was not empty vanity; it rested on a real and demonstrable skill.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for turning aside occurs three times in this single ayah, in three grammatical forms, and it appears in the Quran only in this surah. The concentration is deliberate: the last clause states that the recompense corresponds to the turning away, using the same word for both.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a claim about hypothetical performance by supplying the actual test. Anyone can be confident about what they would do in a situation they are not in, and the ayah quietly points out that the situation has now arrived. The repetition of one verb at the end also makes a point about correspondence: what is returned to a person matches what they did, described in the same word rather than a different one.

crossReferences.why: Records the same boast as a solemn oath, sworn before any warner had reached them.
States the same test earlier in this surah, that insights have come and the seeing is each person's own.
Names the excuse this removes, that they would have asked why no messenger was sent to them.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are confident you would handle better than the person currently handling it. Now recall a time you were given exactly such a chance and did about as well as anybody. Hold the two together for a minute. This ayah's answer to a hypothetical is simply to point at the real one.

studies.title: Faith That Comes Too Late
studies.meaning: Three arrivals are named as things they might be waiting for, and then one of them is followed through. On the day some of your Lord's signs come, faith will not benefit a soul that had not believed before or earned some good through its believing. Commentators discuss which sign is meant and record several readings. What the ayah establishes is a closing point, after which belief is no longer a response to anything but a reaction to what is now visible.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the surah's close, and the demand for a decisive sign has run through the whole of it. The audience had asked for angels and for God Himself to appear. This ayah takes the request seriously enough to describe what would follow if it were granted, and the classical commentators connect it to a wider Quranic account of belief offered at the last moment.

keyTerms.note: The verb for looking and for waiting, used earlier in this surah for the respite granted to people. Waiting and being given time are the same word, which gives the question its edge.

The commercial verb used at the opening of this surah for what God knows of a person. Its appearance here adds a second condition, so belief alone without anything earned through it is not the picture described.
An imperative from the same root as the verb for waiting at the ayah's start. The instruction returns their own posture to them, and the speaker joins it rather than standing outside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Arabia ran to a named term, and a creditor could extend it, but at the moment the term expired the arrangement changed entirely. What had been a negotiation became a claim. Everyone understood that a payment offered the day before and the day after were different acts, and that goodwill did not survive the boundary. The vocabulary of waiting and respite comes from that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes belief arriving too late more than once, including at the drowning of a tyrant who declares his faith as the water closes. Each account uses the same structure: the words are correct, the timing is not, and the passage says plainly that the words no longer do anything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a limit on repentance that is about knowledge rather than about severity. Faith held while the outcome is uncertain is a different act from assent given once the outcome is visible, and only the first is the thing being asked for. The second condition is equally striking. Belief is expected to have produced something, so the ayah measures a life rather than a moment of conviction.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit for repentance offered at the moment death arrives, when nothing is uncertain.
Narrates the clearest instance, a declaration of faith made as the sea closes over the speaker.
Describes faith declared on seeing the punishment, and says it did not benefit them then.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good decision you are postponing until circumstances make it obvious. A resignation, a reconciliation, a change in how you live. Notice that the value of deciding now is precisely that it is not yet obvious. This ayah is about the difference between choosing and conceding, and the window for the first closes quietly.

studies.title: You Have No Part In That
studies.meaning: Two things are described together and the second follows from the first: they broke their religion into pieces, and they became parties. Commentators note that the fracture is named before the factions, so the groups are the result rather than the cause. The instruction is a complete separation from the activity, not from the people, and the reason given is jurisdictional. Their matter rests with God, who will inform them of what they were doing, which is a statement about who does the sorting.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the surah's end, and the classical commentators differ over who is described. Some read it of earlier communities whose unity had fragmented, others as a general statement covering anyone who does this. The tradition preserves the range. The surah has already warned against following many ways instead of one, and this ayah names the outcome of having done so.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for separating something into fragments. The object is their religion, so what is described is damage to a single thing rather than a disagreement between people about it.

The same word used earlier in this surah, where being split into factions is listed among afflictions God is able to send. Its return here makes the condition a consequence rather than only a punishment.
A word covering a matter, a command and a decision at once. Assigning it to God removes the case from human hands entirely, which is the ground of the instruction that precedes it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society was organised into groupings that competed for standing, and a man's identity came from which one claimed him. Splits within a tribe were common and produced long-running rivalries over precedence and inheritance. Everyone knew what it looked like when a body that had been one thing became several, and how quickly the boundary between them became the most important fact about anyone.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for factions in this ayah appears earlier in the same surah, in the list of what God is able to send upon a people, alongside afflictions from above and below. The same term therefore names a punishment in one passage and a self-inflicted condition in the other, without any change of vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the activity from the people doing it, and the separation is what makes the instruction liveable. Judgement is placed with God, explicitly, so what is asked of the reader is only non-participation. That is a narrower demand than it first sounds. It leaves relationships intact, removes the obligation to adjudicate between groups, and identifies the fragmenting itself as the thing to keep clear of.

crossReferences.why: Warns against becoming like those who divided and differed after clear proofs had reached them.
Describes the same outcome, an affair cut into pieces with each party pleased by its own portion.
Gives the instruction this ayah's condition follows from, one path rather than many scattering ways.

studies.applyIt: Notice a dispute within your own community that you have been drawn into by loyalty rather than conviction. Step out of the argument for a month without stepping away from anybody in it. This ayah assigns the judging elsewhere and asks only that you not join the fracturing, which is something you can do quietly.

studies.title: Ten For One
studies.meaning: The rate of exchange is stated plainly, and it is not equal. A good deed brought is answered tenfold. A bad one is answered with its like and no more. Early scholars attend to the wording of both halves. The good is multiplied, and elsewhere in the Quran the ceiling is left open. The bad is capped by a word for equal measure. The closing clause explains why the imbalance is not unfair. Nobody receives less than they earned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a surah largely taken up with argument and warning. Its final verses turn from dispute to a statement of terms, and this is one of them. Early scholars record no occasion for it. They read the placement as deliberate. After a long quarrel about what people had invented, the surah closes by setting out plainly how the account is actually kept.

keyTerms.note: The verb for arriving carrying something, rather than for doing it. It pictures the deed as an item brought to a counter, which is why the response is described as a rate rather than as a verdict.

The multiplier is stated as ten likenesses of the thing itself, not ten of something else. What is returned keeps the shape of what was given, magnified rather than exchanged for a different currency.

The passive of the verb for putting something out of its place. Its use here defines fairness as receiving no less than what is due, which leaves the extra given to a good deed outside the calculation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on rates of exchange, and everyone there understood a multiplier. A merchant financed a caravan expecting several times his outlay back. Profit was reckoned in shares agreed before departure. Putting the moral account in that language used terms the audience handled daily. The tenfold figure would have been heard as a rate of return, not as a picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere raises the multiplier well beyond ten. One passage compares a good deed to a grain that produces seven ears, with a hundred grains in each. It adds that God multiplies further for whom He wills. So the figure of ten here is the floor of what is promised, not its limit. Early scholars read the two together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The imbalance is the teaching. If mercy is written into the accounting itself, hope is not a mood a person has to work up. It is a fact about the ledger. Capping the penalty at equal measure keeps justice intact, so the generosity costs nothing in fairness. Between them the two halves describe a system tilted one way on purpose. The tilt is stated as policy, not as a favour.

crossReferences.why: Raises the same multiplication far higher with the image of a grain and seven ears.
States that God does not wrong by an atom's weight and doubles a good deed.
Repeats the same asymmetry in a Meccan surah, with better than the deed for the good.

studies.applyIt: Do one small good thing today that you would normally skip because it seems too minor to count: a message of thanks, a plate washed that is not yours. The whole argument of this verse is about scale, and it says the scale is not yours to judge. Your part is only the bringing.
studies.explainEasier: If you do one good thing, God gives you ten times as much back. If you do one bad thing, it counts as one, and no more. Nobody is treated unfairly.

studies.title: The Creed Of Abraham
studies.meaning: The declaration is personal and cumulative. My Lord has guided me, and then four descriptions stack up: a straight path, an upright religion, the creed of Abraham, inclining toward truth. Commentators note the word describing that inclination, which names a turning away from everything else and toward one thing at the same time. The final clause is the sharpest, since Abraham is the ancestor the audience claimed and the ayah states plainly that he was not among those who set up partners.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the appeal to Abraham was an appeal to the audience's own genealogy. The families of Mecca traced descent from him and held custody of a sanctuary they associated with him, and their religious practice was defended as inherited from that source. Naming his creed and then denying that it included setting up partners cut directly across that claim.

keyTerms.note: From the root for standing, so a religion described this way is one that stands straight and holds others up. The same root gives the verb used elsewhere for establishing the prayer.
A word for the path a community follows, distinct from the general term for religion. It carries a founder's name naturally, which is why the Quran uses it whenever Abraham is being invoked.

From a root meaning to turn away from something and toward another. Pre-Islamic Arabia knew individuals described by this word who had abandoned the local practices without joining any other community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sources record a small number of men in Mecca and its region before the message who had rejected the local rites and gone looking for the religion of Abraham, some travelling as far as Syria in the search. They were known and regarded as eccentric rather than dangerous. The word used in this ayah for inclining was the term applied to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing Abraham here appears about a dozen times in the Quran, and in almost every case it is immediately followed by a denial that he associated anything with God. The pairing is so consistent that the classical commentators treat the second clause as part of the term's working definition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The declaration answers a claim of inheritance with a claim about content. Descent from Abraham is not disputed; what is disputed is whether the practice being defended is his. That move separates a tradition from the person it is attributed to, and it can be made about any inherited religion. The list also puts guidance first, as something received, before any of the descriptions that follow it.

crossReferences.why: Answers a competing claim with the same phrase, the creed of Abraham, inclining toward truth.
Issues the same instruction to follow that creed, closing with the identical denial about partners.
Describes him as a community in himself, thankful and chosen, and guided to a straight path.

studies.applyIt: Take one practice you keep because it belongs to your tradition and check it against the person or period the tradition claims. Not to reject it if it does not match. Just to know which parts you can trace and which arrived later. This ayah makes exactly that distinction about a lineage everyone in the room shared.

studies.title: My Living And My Dying
studies.meaning: Four things are named and handed over in a single clause: prayer, offering, life and death. The first two are acts of worship. The second two are not acts at all, which is what makes the list unusual. Early scholars read it as extending devotion past what a person does, into what merely happens to them. The declaration then closes with a claim about being first. They explain that as first among this community rather than in history.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It is the closing declaration of a surah that has argued at length with people who dedicated animals and crops to various powers. The instruction to say this is therefore pointed. The practices disputed throughout the surah are exactly the ones being reassigned here. Early scholars read these verses as the surah's summing up, delivered in the first person rather than as one more argument.

keyTerms.note: A word for the animal offered and for acts of devotion generally. Its root also carries washing and purity, so the term joins a physical offering to the idea of being made clean.
A noun for the whole of a life rather than for the act of living. Paired with its counterpart it covers the span a person does not control, placing that under the same dedication as their prayer.

Early scholars explain first as foremost within this community rather than earliest in time, since the Quran describes earlier prophets in the same terms. It marks priority of commitment, not chronology.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Animals were dedicated by name in Arabia before Islam. A camel might be marked for a particular god. Its ear was slit and its milk kept back. A slaughter was announced with the name of the power it was offered to. Everyone present heard whose it was. In that setting, declaring who an offering was for was a public act of allegiance, not a private intention.
studies.didYouKnow: These two verses are among the passages many Muslims recite inside the prayer itself. They come in the opening supplication reported in the classical collections. So a statement that begins with the word prayer ends up being spoken during one. Early scholars note that circle when they discuss where the passage came to be used.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined by range rather than by strength of feeling. The list moves from what a person does to what simply happens. So what is offered includes the parts of a life nobody chooses and nobody can perform. That makes the declaration impossible to complete by effort. That is the point of it. It is a statement of ownership, not a report of achievement. The denial of any partner then restates the same sentence.

crossReferences.why: Describes sincere devotion as the whole of what was ever commanded.
Uses the same language of turning one's face over to God while doing good.
States that the flesh of offerings does not reach God, only the awareness behind them.

studies.applyIt: Before something ordinary today, say quietly who it is for. A meal, a commute, opening your laptop. Not a long formula. These verses put living and dying in the same list as prayer. So the offering is meant to cover the plain hours. Those are the ones nobody thinks to dedicate.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to say that his prayer, his worship, his life and his death all belong to God alone. God has no partner. That is what he has been told to say.

studies.title: Shall I Seek Another Lord
studies.meaning: The question echoes one asked near the surah's beginning and answers it the same way: He is the Lord of everything, so there is nothing left over to be lord of anything. Then two clauses about responsibility, the second of which has become one of the most quoted lines in the Quran. No soul earns except against itself, and no bearer of burdens carries another's. Commentators read the pair together, since the first makes accountability personal and the second makes it non-transferable.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical sources record that opponents in the city offered to carry the consequences of the believers' conduct if they would return to the old religion. The Quran answers such offers elsewhere in similar terms. Whether or not this ayah responds to a specific instance, the arrangement it rules out was a live proposal in a society where a clan absorbed its members' liabilities.

keyTerms.note: The verb for seeking something out, from a root that also produces the word for overstepping. Seeking beyond what is there and going past a limit share the same letters in Arabic.
From the root for a heavy pack, which this surah used earlier for burdens carried on the back. The verb and its object share the root, so the Arabic says a bearer does not bear a bearing.
From a root for coming after or succeeding one another, so disagreement is pictured as positions taken in turn. What is promised at the end is information about the difference, not a rebuke for it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Liability in Arabia was collective by design. A clan paid the compensation for a killing by one of its members and collected for injuries to any of them, and this pooling was the whole security of life without a state. A man genuinely could take on another's debt. The offer to carry someone's consequences was therefore an ordinary transaction, not a rhetorical flourish.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that no bearer carries another's burden appears five times in the Quran, in five different surahs, always in nearly identical words. Few sentences are repeated that consistently, and the classical commentaries treat the repetition as establishing a principle rather than answering any single occasion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas that pull in opposite directions are held in one ayah. God is Lord of everything, which is the largest possible claim, and each soul carries only its own load, which is the smallest possible unit. The combination rules out both a universe with several authorities and a community that can absorb an individual's account. What is left is a direct relationship with nothing and nobody standing in the middle of it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same principle and adds that a heavily laden soul finds nobody to carry any of it.
States it as one of the contents of the earlier scriptures, at the head of a short list.
Records the offer to carry another's faults and says the offer will not be honoured.

studies.applyIt: Think of a responsibility you have quietly handed to someone else: a decision you let a parent make, a moral question you outsourced to an institution. Take one of them back this week and decide it yourself. This ayah says the load is not transferable, which means the decision was never actually theirs to hold.

studies.title: Successors Upon The Earth
studies.meaning: The surah closes by naming what human beings are: those who come after, placed on the earth in succession, with some raised above others in degrees. The purpose given for the difference is a test, and the test is in what has been given rather than in what has been withheld. Commentators note that the inequality itself is described as the trial. Two closing names then hold the ending open at both ends, one of swift consequence and one of forgiveness and mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the final ayah of a surah that has argued for a hundred and sixty-five ayat about who God is and what may be said in His name. The audience held rank in a city built on it. Naming their arrangement as a test rather than a verdict is the last thing the surah says to them, and it neither abolishes the ranks nor endorses them.

keyTerms.note: The plural of one who comes after another, from the root for succession. The word names people by their position in a sequence rather than by any authority, so it describes a turn rather than a title.
Steps of a stair, the third appearance of this word in the surah. It has already been used for a prophet's raising and for the grading of outcomes, and here it names ordinary social difference.
From a root meaning to wear something out by use, as a garment is tested by being worn. A trial in this vocabulary reveals what a thing is made of rather than punishing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on visible degrees. Some families held the sanctuary's offices, some financed caravans, some worked them, and some were owned. Nobody imagined the arrangement could be otherwise, and the differences were displayed daily in seating, in speech and in who greeted whom first. To describe that whole structure as a set of examination conditions was to say something no one there had heard.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for degrees appears three times in this surah, applied first to a prophet being raised, then to the grading of every person by what they did, and finally here to social rank. The same term therefore covers spiritual elevation, moral outcome and worldly position within one surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Inequality is neither justified nor abolished but reassigned a purpose, which is a harder and more useful position than either alternative. Whoever holds more is holding a test rather than a reward, and whoever holds less is in the same examination with a different paper. The two closing names then keep the ending unresolved on purpose, since a surah about accountability finishes with forgiveness as its last word.

crossReferences.why: Names the same role at the beginning of the human story, one placed on the earth in succession.
States the same purpose for life and death, a test of which of you is better in conduct.
Gives a reason for the raising in degrees, so that people may make use of one another.

studies.applyIt: Take one advantage you hold that you did not earn: where you were born, an education, a body that works. Name it as an examination question rather than a possession, and ask what it is asking of you. This is the surah's last word, and it turns a fact about your life into something addressed to you.
